issues.title: Connect GitHub or GitLab
issues.description:
Connect your account to link issues to pull/merge requests and automate your workflow:

* Link Linear issues to pull requests.
* Automatically update an issue's status when PRs are created or merged.
* Connect one or multiple repos.

[Connect GitHub or GitLab →](https://linear.app/settings/integrations/github)

## Setup tips

#### How to link a Linear issue to a PR

* **Branch name** (e.g. "LIN-123" or "username/LIN-123"). To quickly copy branch name for an issue to your clipboard, press `Cmd/Ctrl` `Shift` `.`
* **Pull request title** (e.g. "GitHub Workflow LIN-123")
* **Pull request description** (e.g. *Fixes LIN-123, Resolves LIN-123*) – it will not work if entered in commits or comments.

#### When you link a Linear issue to a PR, Linear will:

* Create a link to the PR in the Linear issue.
* Comment on the PR with a link back to the Linear issue.
* Once PR has been opened, Linear will change the status of the issue to "In Progress".
* Once PR has been merged, Linear will change the status of the issue as "Done".

#### Suggested Workflow

1. Select or create the issue you want to work on next.
2. Open the command menu (`Cmd` `K` on Mac, or `Ctrl` `K` on Windows) and select **Copy git branch name,** or use the shortcut `Cmd/Ctrl` `Shift` `.`
3. This will copy the git branch name to your clipboard (e.g. `username/LIN-123-github-workflow`
4. Paste the branch name to your git checkout command to create a new branch: `git checkout -b username/LIN-123-github-workflow`
5. Make your changes and push the branch to GitHub and open a pull request
6. Once the pull request is open, Linear will comment on the PR and change the issue state to **In Progress***.* 
7. Once the PR merged, Linear will change the status to Done.

Read full integration instructions for [GitHub](https://linear.app/docs/github) and [GitLab →](https://linear.app/docs/gitlab)

ClickHouse DATABASE_URL uses unsupported /database-name path syntax
issues.description:
We inject a `DATABASE_URL` like this for ClickHouse services:

```
clickhouse://default:4Oba-3IypRfH9auAAFQLfYKJnbDwWtNc@clickhouse-clickhouse-s9jot1u6iwl9.unbind-user:9000/default
```

That's wrong — ClickHouse doesn't accept the `/database-name` path syntax, so anything consuming the injected URL as-is fails to connect.

**Where it's built (two places, must be fixed together):**

* `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/database_secrets.go:157` — `DATABASE_URL` (and `DATABASE_HTTP_URL` on the next line, same `/default` suffix on port 8123)
* `apps/operator/internal/controller/credentials.go:187` — `updateClickhouseSecretData`, same format string for both the native and HTTP URL

**To do:**

* Decide the correct DSN form (e.g. drop the path entirely, or express the database as a query param like `?database=default`) and confirm it works against a real ClickHouse instance.
* Apply the same fix to `DATABASE_HTTP_URL`.
* Existing ClickHouse services already have the bad URL stored in their secret — make sure the fix rewrites the value on reconcile rather than only applying to newly created databases.
* `DATABASE_DEFAULT_DB_NAME`, `DATABASE_HOST`, `DATABASE_PORT` are already injected separately, so the database name is still available to consumers regardless of what we do with the URL.

---

**Client context: it's the JS client (**`@clickhouse/clickhouse-js`**).**

Checked the docs — the documented URL format is:

```
http[s]://[username:password@]hostname:port[/database][?param1=value1&param2=value2]
```

So for the JS client specifically:

* The `/database-name` path is **fine** — a pathname provided directly in `url` is parsed as the `database` option. (There's a separate `pathname` config param for reverse-proxy sub-paths so the two don't collide.)
* What actually breaks it is the **scheme and port**: the client is HTTP-only. It doesn't understand `clickhouse://` and doesn't speak the native protocol on 9000. It wants `http://` on 8123 (or `https://` on 8443).

Which means our existing `DATABASE_HTTP_URL` (`http://default:<pass>@<host>:8123/default`) is already the correct shape for this client — the problem is that `DATABASE_URL` is the obvious name to reach for and it hands you a DSN the JS client can't use.

**Revised direction — worth deciding before changing the DSN format:**

* Is the real fix to make `DATABASE_URL` discoverable/pointed at the HTTP endpoint for ClickHouse, rather than rewriting the native DSN's path?
* If we still want to change the native DSN, confirm which client actually rejects `/default` first — `clickhouse-go`'s DSN parser does accept it, so the original diagnosis may not apply to the native URL at all.
* Either way, document which of the two URLs a consumer should use for ClickHouse.

issues.title: UNBIND_INTERNAL_URL is wrong for Meilisearch (and the resolved value isn't visible anywhere)
issues.description:
The `UNBIND_INTERNAL_URL` we hand out for a Meilisearch service is wrong, but we can't say exactly how — the resolved value isn't surfaced anywhere in the UI, so there's no way to inspect what actually got injected.

**Two parts to this:**

1. **Make the resolved internal URL visible.** Internal endpoint references render as `UNBIND_INTERNAL_URL` in the variables UI (`apps/web/src/components/variables/helpers.ts:43`) but only show the reference, not the resolved value. Without that, debugging is guesswork. This is the blocker for part 2.
2. **Fix the value for Meilisearch.** Once we can see it, figure out what's wrong and fix it.

**Where the value comes from:** `resolveInternalEndpointURL` in `apps/api/internal/services/variables/resolve_references.go:136`. It picks the first TCP port on the endpoint, then:

* non-database services → `http://<dns>:<port>`
* database services → bare DNS, no scheme, no port

Meilisearch is a `dockerimage` template service (`apps/api/pkg/templates/meilisearch.go`) exposing TCP 7700, so it should land in the first branch and produce `http://<dns>:7700`. Suspects worth checking: which port gets picked when there's more than one, whether the DNS value is the short or fully-qualified name, and whether the scheme/port is what a Meili client actually expects.

Re-run service icon detection when the git branch changes
issues.description:
## Problem

Service icon (`config.icon`) and railpack provider/framework are detected only once, at GitHub-service creation, and always against the repo's **default** branch (`apps/api/internal/services/service/create.go:189-222`). Changing the branch later persists it without re-running detection, so a service switched to a branch with a different stack keeps a stale icon (and stale `SERVICE_PROVIDER`/`SERVICE_FRAMEWORK` build env vars).

Detection should follow the **selected** branch:

* Draft services start on the default branch, so creation-time analysis stays as is.
* Changing the branch — in the draft panel or in deployed settings — re-runs detection and updates icon/provider/framework. No loading placeholder; the icon just refreshes when done.
* Not per build: each detection costs a shallow clone, and the builder already clones every build. Branch changes are the meaningful signal; re-detecting only then gives the same freshness at human frequency. For a deployed branch change the API-side clone is redundant with the rebuild's clone, but builder-side detection would need a new report-back path and wouldn't cover drafts (no build runs there) — one code path wins.

Verified safety facts:

* Calling the update endpoint on a draft service does **not** trigger a deployment (`NeedsDeployment` returns `NoDeploymentNeeded` with no current deployment, `internal/repositories/service/queries.go:308-310`).
* No manual icon override exists in `UpdateServiceInput`, so overwriting the icon is safe.
* Branch change on a deployed service already triggers a rebuild via `NeedsDeployment`'s `GitBranch` comparison.

## API (`apps/api`)

1. **Extract helper** `analyzeGitRepository(ctx, installationID, owner, repo, branch)` (new `internal/services/service/git_analysis.go`): `GetInstallationByID` → `VerifyRepositoryAccess` (empty branch → default) → shallow `CloneRepository("refs/heads/"+branch)` → `AnalyzeSourceCode`. Refactor `create.go:189-222` to use it (create keeps hard-failing; return the installation for `gitOwnerName`).

Longhorn storage leaks: retained PVs and expand snapshots silently fill the disk
issues.description:
Debugged a real install: 300 GB disk at 77% (later 91%) full while the UI showed only ~30 GB of volumes. All of the hidden usage traced back to how we configure Longhorn. Three separate problems:

## 1. Deleted volumes never free disk space

The installer sets the default Longhorn storage class to `reclaimPolicy: Retain` (`apps/installer/internal/k3s/install.go` and `deploy/charts/environments/default.yaml`). So deleting a PVC leaves a `Released` PV and the full Longhorn volume on disk, forever. There is no UI or cleanup path for these — they are invisible leaked disk.

On the debugged server this had accumulated **~187 GB across 12 orphaned volumes** from normal delete/recreate cycles of services (5 generations of meilisearch, 4 of clickhouse, 4 of redis).

**Decision made:** keep `Retain` as the default (safety net for cascaded/accidental deletions), but an explicit volume delete in the UI must actually destroy the volume.

**Status: fix implemented (uncommitted). **`DeletePersistentVolumeClaim` in `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/persistentvolumeclaims.go` now verifies the bound PV's `claimRef` points at the PVC, patches the PV to `Delete`, then deletes the PVC; on PVC-delete failure it reverts the policy. Tests added.

Note this only covers the explicit volume-delete path. Service/environment/project deletion still leaks volume data by design (operator cascade deletes PVCs, PVs are retained). We may want a follow-up: release PVs when a service is deliberately deleted, and/or surface Released PVs somewhere.

## 2. Volume expansion pins a full copy of the data, every time

Longhorn takes a system snapshot named `expand-<size>` on every volume expansion and nothing ever purges it. Growing a volume in the UI therefore freezes the whole dataset at that moment. Users grow volumes exactly when data is growing fast, so this compounds: on the debugged server, a 65 Gi meilisearch volume with 48 GB of real data held **195 GB on disk** (6 resizes in one day = ~149 GB of frozen history); clickhouse was 3x its size too.

**Status: not fixed.** Proposed: API deletes the `expand-<size>` snapshot after a successful resize (identifiable by name + volume), and/or ship Longhorn `RecurringJob` CRs (`snapshot-cleanup` + `filesystem-trim`) attached to the `default` group so all volumes get periodic compaction. Also worth reviewing `auto-cleanup-system-generated-snapshot` and `snapshot-max-count` defaults.

## 3. No visibility

The UI shows requested PVC sizes only. Actual Longhorn usage (snapshots, retained orphans) is invisible, so users can't explain or fix a full disk. Worth considering surfacing actual per-volume disk usage and orphaned/Released storage.

## Manual recovery used (for reference / docs)

```bash
# orphaned Released PVs: delete Longhorn volume + PV record
kubectl get pv --no-headers | awk '$5=="Released" {print $1}'
kubectl -n longhorn-system delete volumes.longhorn.io <name> && kubectl delete pv <name>

# expansion snapshots: delete, Longhorn purges/coalesces in background
kubectl -n longhorn-system get snapshots.longhorn.io -o name | grep 'expand-' \
  | xargs kubectl -n longhorn-system delete
```

Registry volume is 4Gi and the cleanup job is broken — builds fail with "no space left on device". Also, 4Gi might be too small, consider 10GB.
issues.description:
Owners: @bbedward and @ngyekta (Linear only allows one assignee, so both are named here).

## Symptom

Builds fail at the push step even on nodes with plenty of free disk (reported case had ~150 GB free on the host):

```
ERROR Buildkit: task exporting to image failed: failed to push docker-registry.unbind-system:5000/tezara:e04be9ca4d24-366ed82277ca:
  unknown: unknown error - filesystem: mkdir /var/lib/registry/docker/registry/v2/repositories/tezara/_uploads/01a04fbe-...: no space left on device
FATAL Failed to build with docker: build failed: failed to solve: ...
```

## Root cause

The node's free space is irrelevant. The registry writes to its own fixed-size volume, and we default it to **4Gi**.

`deploy/charts/environments/default.yaml:71-77`

```yaml
registry:
  persistence:
    size: 4Gi
  cleanup:
    threshold: 3Gi
```

That becomes `registry-pvc` (`deploy/charts/charts/registry/templates/pvc.yaml`) with no `storageClassName`, so it lands on the default class — Longhorn, which the installer makes default by stripping the annotation off `local-path` (`apps/installer/internal/k3s/install.go:874-882`). A Longhorn volume is a fixed-size ext4 block device, so it returns `ENOSPC` at 4Gi no matter how empty the host is.

## Why 4Gi runs out fast

Images **and** build cache share the same volume. `apps/api/pkg/builder/internal/buildkit/buildkit.go:287-294` exports cache as `type=registry, mode=max`, which writes every intermediate layer — commonly several times the size of the final image. Every build also pushes a new immutable tag (`e04be9ca4d24-366ed82277ca`). A single service with a ~1 GB image can consume the whole volume by itself.

## Why the hourly cleanup doesn't save us

Four separate problems in `deploy/charts/charts/registry/templates/cleanup_cron.yaml`:

1. **The job dies on repos with no tags.** Line 30 sets `set -e`; lines 127 and 272 do `TAGS=$(curl ... | jq -r '.tags[]')`. When a repo's tag list is `null`, jq exits 5, and errexit applies to the assignment — the script aborts before ever reaching the `if [ -z "$TAGS" ]` guard directly below it. Verified. Null-tag repos are exactly what distribution leaves behind after GC removes all manifests (it never deletes the repo directory) and after a failed push. So a failed push creates the very condition that permanently wedges cleanup — a self-reinforcing loop.
2. `SPACE_FREED` **is computed from a stale variable.** Line 315: `ESTIMATED_TAG_SIZE=$((REPO_SIZE / TAG_COUNT))` reads `REPO_SIZE`, which is left over from the *sizing* loop (line 158) and holds the last repo measured there, not the repo currently being cleaned. If that stale value is large, the loop hits its budget after one delete and stops early.
3. **Only 1Gi of headroom, checked hourly.** A 3Gi threshold on a 4Gi volume. One build between cron runs clears that gap.
4. **"Preserve latest tag" is wrong for our tag format.** Lines 275-278 fall back to `sort -V | tail -n 1`. Version-sorting a hex tag like `e04be9ca4d24-366ed82277ca` is meaningless, so it preserves an arbitrary tag and can delete the manifest for the image actually running. Running pods survive, but restarts and rescheduling break.

Also fragile: the job runs `apt-get update` and installs kubectl from the internet on every run (lines 36-42) under `set -e`, so any apt or network hiccup silently skips cleanup entirely.

## What to fix

- [ ] Raise the default registry volume size well above 4Gi and set the cleanup threshold to ~80% of it.
- [ ] Fix the `set -e` + `jq '.tags[]'` abort on null-tag repos (handle `.tags[]?` or `// empty`).
- [ ] Fix the stale `REPO_SIZE` in the space-freed estimate.
- [ ] Replace `sort -V` tag ordering with something correct for our tag format, and never delete the manifest for a deployed image.
- [ ] Stop installing kubectl from the internet on every cleanup run — bake it into an image or drop the dependency.
- [ ] **Expose registry cache settings in the UI. **`/cache/registry/config`, `/cache/registry/stats` and `/cache/registry/update` already exist (`apps/api/internal/api/handlers/system/system.go:117-138`), but nothing in `apps/web/src` calls them outside the generated client. An operator hitting this today has no way to see usage or grow the volume from the dashboard.
- [ ] **Persist PVC capacity. **`persistRegistryCacheSettings` (`apps/api/internal/services/system/registry_cache.go:170-188`) saves only threshold and schedule, not `PVCCapacityGB`. After a helm upgrade the chart re-applies `4Gi` against a now-larger PVC; Kubernetes forbids shrinking, so the upgrade errors out.
- [ ] Consider bounding buildkit's `mode=max` cache export, or giving the build cache its own volume so it can't starve image pushes.

## Unrelated latent issue spotted nearby

`deploy/charts/charts/registry/templates/deployment.yaml` has no `strategy: Recreate` on a RWO volume, so a registry rollout can deadlock with the new pod stuck waiting to attach.

## Operator workaround until this ships

```bash
kubectl -n unbind-system exec deploy/docker-registry -- \
  /bin/registry garbage-collect /etc/distribution/config.yml --delete-untagged=true

kubectl -n unbind-system exec deploy/docker-registry -- \
  sh -c 'rm -rf /var/lib/registry/docker/registry/v2/repositories/*/_uploads/*'

kubectl -n unbind-system patch pvc registry-pvc \
  -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"60Gi"}}}}'
```

Then raise `MAX_STORAGE` on the `registry-cleanup` CronJob to match, or cleanup will fire constantly.

issues.title: Postgres deployments always flip to ERROR after 5 min (stale unbind-deployment pod label)
issues.description:
## Symptom

A healthy Zalando Postgres service shows its current deployment as **ERROR** in the UI while the pod health icons are green and both deploy logs and build logs are clean. Reproduced on a live deployment: current deployment "via Database Operator" completes in ~3s, then flips to ERROR ~5 minutes later. Every subsequent deployment does the same, forever.

## Root cause

The ERROR chip is `launch-error`, which the API computes live for the current deployment in `calculateInstanceData` (`apps/api/internal/services/deployments/instance_data.go`):

1. If **any** pod of the service carries an `unbind-deployment` label, only pods whose label equals the current deployment ID are counted (`instance_data.go:100`).
2. If none match, `noCurrentPods` kicks in: LAUNCHING during a 5-minute grace period, then `launch-error` with "No pods from the current deployment after 5m0s; rollout may be stuck" (`instance_data.go:199-205`).

For Postgres that label can never match, because it is **permanently stale**:

* Zalando's `inherited_labels` (`deploy/charts/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl:390`) copies `unbind-deployment` from the `postgresql` CR down to pods.
* But the operator never updates CR labels after creation: `reconcilePostgresql` (`apps/operator/internal/controller/dependents.go:40-48`) applies only `existing.Spec = desired.Spec`. The render hash includes metadata, so the update path fires, writes a new hash annotation, and still leaves the old labels in place.
* So the CR — and the pods — keep the deployment ID from when the CR was first created. Every new deployment of a postgres service is guaranteed to hit the grace-period timeout.

## Why everything else looks healthy

* Instance/heart icons use `GetInstanceHealth` (`apps/api/internal/services/instances/status.go:45`), which selects pods by `unbind-service` only → correctly healthy.
* Deploy logs for the current deployment fall back to service-level logs (`apps/api/internal/services/logs/logs.go:207-211` — comment there already notes "never-rolled pods keep the previous rollout's unbind-deployment label") → clean logs.
* The stale-label problem was already worked around for redis (`pkg/databases/assets/definitions/databases/redis/definition.yaml:65-69` excludes `unbind-deployment` from pod labels) and clickhouse, but postgres label propagation is controlled by Zalando operator config, not the template. The status gating landed in `31a44b16` (Aug 25, 2026).

## Suggested fix

1. Drop `unbind-deployment` from Zalando's `inherited_labels` in the helmfile — then `anyPodHasDeploymentLabel` is false for postgres and the gate falls back to counting all service pods (matches what redis/clickhouse already do).
2. Optionally also sync labels onto existing CRs in the `reconcileResource` mutators so the label tracks the latest deployment when pods do roll.

Related secondary path worth checking while in there: `applyDatabaseCRStatus` (`instance_data.go:216`) flips a healthy DB to `launch-error` when the Zalando CR reports `SyncFailed`/`UpdateFailed`, which Zalando sets for non-fatal sync hiccups while the cluster keeps running.

issues.title: Builds silently break when pnpm skips optional deps; cache/no-cache UX made it undebuggable
issues.description:
## What happened

bambu-dashboard `apps/web` failed every build with `Cannot find module '@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu'`. Root cause was app-side, not unbind: `engines.node: ">=20"` made railpack pick node 20.20.2, while `@tanstack/react-start` requires node >=22.12. Under railpack's default build env (`CI=true`, `NODE_ENV=production` — railpack `core/providers/node/node.go:394,400`), pnpm doesn't fail on the engine mismatch — it **silently skips the optional deps** of the affected subtree (`skipped-optional-dependency … reason: unsupported_engine`, debug-level only), dropping the rolldown/esbuild/lightningcss native bindings vite 8 needs. Fix on the app side: bump `engines.node` to `>=22.12`.

## Unbind improvements worth extracting

1. **"Skip cache" doesn't skip railpack cache mounts. **`DisableBuildCache` sets `IgnoreCache` on LLB ops and drops registry cache imports (`apps/api/pkg/builder/internal/buildkit/buildkit.go:254-286`), but BuildKit cache *mounts* (railpack's pnpm store etc.) still mount their persistent contents. Railpack's escape hatch `RAILPACK_DISABLE_CACHES` is read from the builder's process env (`build_llb/build_graph.go:396-400`) and unbind never sets it. Fix: when `disable_build_cache` is set, also set `RAILPACK_DISABLE_CACHES=*` in the builder job env (next to `DISABLE_BUILD_CACHE` in `apps/api/internal/deployctl/deployctl.go:473-475`). During this incident "Skip cache" not ruling out cache-mount state cost a lot of debugging time.
2. **buildkitd storage is** `emptyDir` (`deploy/charts/charts/buildkitd/templates/deployment.yaml`) — any pod reschedule silently drops the whole build cache. Since the cache is that disposable anyway, a "clear build cache" button (delete buildkitd pod or `buildctl prune`) would be cheap and would give users a real recovery path.
3. **Surface pnpm's skipped-optional-dependency warnings.** pnpm only reveals the engine-based skip at debug level; the build then fails much later with a misleading native-binding error that looks like cache corruption or an arch mismatch. A build-log heuristic (or passing `--loglevel=warn`-equivalent reporting for install steps) that flags "optional dependency skipped: unsupported engine/platform" would have pointed at the root cause immediately. Related: consider warning when the resolved node version doesn't satisfy the engines of the app's direct dependencies.

## Debugging notes (for posterity)

* Identical failure across: fresh buildkitd (emptyDir wipe), "Skip cache" deploys, and registry cache — because it was deterministic, not cache.
* Reproduction: `CI=true` (or `NODE_ENV=production`) + node 20.20.2 + pnpm 10.6.2 + this lockfile → 609 packages, no bindings; same install under node >=22.12 → 627 packages, bindings present. Verified with the exact corepack pnpm tarball and node build the builder uses.

issues.title: Internal service hostnames are short-form (name.namespace) — breaks clients that bypass search domains
issues.description:
Everywhere we hand users an internal hostname, we emit the short form `<kube-name>.<namespace>` instead of the FQDN `<kube-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.

The short form is not a real DNS record. It only resolves because the pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` search domains + `ndots:5` make the OS resolver retry with `.svc.cluster.local` appended. Any client that bypasses the system resolver queries the literal name, gets NXDOMAIN, and fails.

**Real-world hit:** Chromium (its built-in async DNS resolver ignores search domains) inside a service failed with `net::ERR_PROXY_CONNECTION_FAILED` against the gluetun template's proxy URL. curl in the same pod worked, which makes this miserable to debug. Same class of failure applies to anything with DNS-over-HTTPS enabled or a custom resolver.

**Where we emit short-form hosts:**

* `apps/api/internal/services/templates/deploy.go:344` — `IsHost` + `ResolveAsNormalVariable` template references resolve to `%s.%s` (kubeName, namespace).
* `apps/operator/internal/controller/credentials.go:147` — Postgres `DATABASE_HOST` = `name.namespace`.
* `apps/operator/internal/controller/credentials.go:162` — MySQL `DATABASE_HOST` = `moco-name.namespace`.
* `apps/operator/internal/controller/database.go:206-208` — Redis `DATABASE_HOST` and `DATABASE_URL` = `name-headless.namespace`.
* Template definitions using `${SERVICE_X_KUBE_NAME}.${NAMESPACE}` in StringReplace values (gluetun already fixed to FQDN; audit the rest).
* Runtime host reference resolution in `apps/api/internal/services/variables/` — audit alongside the deploy-time path.
* `apps/api/internal/services/service/dns.go:132` — the "internal URL" shown in the UI for every service (`%s.%s` kubeName, namespace).
* `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/dns_discovery.go:62` — endpoint discovery `DNS` field, which also feeds available variable references.

**Fix:** append `.svc.cluster.local` at every emission point. FQDNs resolve identically for search-domain-aware clients, so this is backward compatible for connection strings we generate. Caveat: `DATABASE_HOST` values are stored in live k8s secrets and users may have copied them elsewhere — changing the operator's emission updates secrets on reconcile, which is the desired behavior, but release notes should mention it.

Old container images/layer snapshots accumulate on nodes and fill up disk
issues.description:
On a single-node Unbind install, `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/containerd` had grown to **80G** (out of 205G total disk usage on a 301G disk). Every git-based deployment builds and pushes a new image, and old images/layer snapshots pile up in containerd's cache indefinitely — nothing in Unbind prunes them.

:This eventually causes disk pressure. In this case it likely contributed to a Longhorn volume getting remounted read-only, which put a Meilisearch service into a crash loop (`Read-only file system (os error 30)`).

Manual workaround today: `k3s crictl rmi --prune` on the node, which is not something users should have to know about.

Possible directions:

* Ensure kubelet image GC is configured/working with sane thresholds on Unbind installs
* Periodic prune job (old build images, buildkit cache) shipped by Unbind
* Retention policy for old deployment images in the self-hosted registry as well, since it grows unboundedly for the same reason

---

**Related: Longhorn expansion snapshots are never cleaned up either.**

When a volume is expanded through Unbind, Longhorn automatically takes a system snapshot (`volume-snap-expand-<size>.img`) before resizing — and nothing ever deletes it. The snapshot pins the entire pre-expansion state, so every block the app rewrites afterward goes into the volume head instead of being overwritten in place.

Real case from the same node: a Meilisearch volume expanded to 55Gi had an `expand-59055800320` snapshot pinning a full 55Gi of dead history — the replica directory was **86G of actual disk for a 55Gi volume** (worst case ~2x volume size). For write-heavy workloads (databases, search indexes) this invisibly doubles the disk cost of any volume that has ever been resized.

Fix: after a successful expansion, the operator should delete the expansion system snapshot (Longhorn snapshot CRD/API) once the volume is healthy, and ideally run a filesystem trim afterward.

**Implementation gotcha for the snapshot cleanup:** deleting the `snapshots.longhorn.io` CR alone does NOT reclaim the space — it only marks the snapshot as removed, and the engine's purge never fires (`purgeStatus` stays `isPurging: false`). The actual reclaim had to be kicked by creating and immediately deleting a throwaway Snapshot CR on the volume, which triggers a purge cycle that prunes the removed expand-snapshot. Whatever the operator does here needs to trigger the purge explicitly (or use the Longhorn API's SnapshotPurge call) rather than just deleting the CR.

Also worth evaluating the Longhorn global setting `remove-snapshots-during-filesystem-trim` — with it enabled, a filesystem trim also removes snapshots marked as removed (dropping their stale blocks), so the cleanup could be: mark expansion snapshot removed, trigger trim, done in one pass. Unbind could enable this setting by default at install time.

Assigning a backup bucket to a deployed database never reaches the cluster
issues.description:
## Problem

Assigning an S3 backup bucket to an already-deployed Postgres database in the service settings saves the bucket ID on the service config, but the running Zalando cluster never receives the WAL-G env vars. No backups are ever taken. Reproduced by assigning a bucket and waiting a full day with nothing showing up in the bucket.

## Cause

Two gaps combine on the update path:

1. `NeedsDeployment` in `apps/api/internal/repositories/service/queries.go` compares the old and new CRD on a fixed list of fields (hosts, replicas, ports, run command, volumes, health check, resources, ...). The database spec, including `S3BackupConfig`, is not part of the comparison. After picking a bucket the two CRDs are equal, so it returns "no deployment needed" and nothing is redeployed.
2. Even if a redeploy did happen, `CreateCRDFromService` in `apps/api/internal/services/deployments/redeploy.go` starts from the previous deployment's stored resource definition and only overwrites the database config, hosts, ports, etc. It never sets `Spec.Config.Database.S3BackupConfig` from the service config.

The only path that wires the bucket into the CRD is the full build path: `populateDatabaseEnv` in `apps/api/internal/deployctl/deployctl.go` exports the `SERVICE_DATABASE_BACKUP_*` env vars and the builder turns them into the spec in `apps/api/pkg/builder/k8s/crd.go`. Assigning the bucket at creation time works for the same reason.

## How to confirm

```
kubectl get postgresql -n <team-namespace> <cluster> -o yaml | grep -E "WAL_S3_BUCKET|BACKUP_SCHEDULE|USE_WALG_BACKUP"
```

If those env vars are missing, this is the bug. Triggering a full rebuild of the database service is a workaround since it goes through the builder.

## Proposed fix

* Include the database spec (at least `S3BackupConfig`, schedule and retention) in the `NeedsDeployment` comparison so a bucket change triggers a redeploy.
* Set `S3BackupConfig` from the service config in `CreateCRDFromService` so the ad-hoc redeploy carries the bucket, secret name, schedule and retention into the CRD. Clearing the bucket should also clear it.

issues.description:
## Problem

Creating a database service with a display name that contains a space (for example `my pg`) succeeds, but the first deployment fails with a 500:

```
failed to create PersistentVolumeClaim 'pgdata-my-pg-wenu6bufg9pt-0' in namespace 'default-b4b7woh2v3md': PersistentVolumeClaim "pgdata-my-pg-wenu6bufg9pt-0" is invalid: metadata.labels: Invalid value: "my pg": a valid label must be an empty string or consist of alphanumeric characters, '-', '_' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character
```

Renaming the service to a hyphenated name makes the deploy go through. Found while verifying [UNB-263](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-263/assigning-a-backup-bucket-to-a-deployed-database-never-reaches-the).

## Cause

`dbvolumes.Ensure` in `apps/api/internal/dbvolumes/dbvolumes.go` passes `service.Name` as the display name when pre-creating the database claims. `CreatePersistentVolumeClaim` in `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/persistentvolumeclaims.go` writes that value verbatim into the `pvc-display-name` label. Kubernetes label values cannot contain spaces, so any display name with a space (or other characters outside `[A-Za-z0-9-_.]`) is rejected.

The UI only checks length on service names (`ServiceNameSchema` in `apps/web/src/lib/queries/update-service-input.ts`, 2 to 32 characters), so this is reachable from the normal create flow. The API does not validate the name either.

## Proposed fix

Stop using the free-form display name as a label value. Either store it in an annotation instead, or sanitize it into a valid label value before setting it. Also check the other `CreatePersistentVolumeClaim` callers (user-created PVCs via `/storage/pvc/create`) since they hit the same code path.

issues.title: Existing installs never receive the new kubelet image GC and eviction settings
issues.description:
Follow-up to [UNB-259](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-259/old-container-imageslayer-snapshots-accumulate-on-nodes-and-fill-up). The installer now writes a full kubelet config (`imageGCHighThresholdPercent: 75`, `imageGCLowThresholdPercent: 65`, `imageMaximumGCAge: 72h`, disk-based `evictionHard` signals), but only fresh installs get it. Nothing rewrites `/etc/rancher/k3s/kubelet-config.yaml` on nodes that were installed earlier, and the in-app updater runs inside the cluster and cannot touch host files or restart k3s.

Existing nodes therefore still run with image GC at 85%/80%, no maximum image age, and memory-only eviction. The node [UNB-259](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-259/old-container-imageslayer-snapshots-accumulate-on-nodes-and-fill-up) was filed from is one of these: its disk was at 68%, so even the new 75% threshold would not fire there. The 72h age limit is what actually fixes the accumulation, and existing installs never get it.

## Why rewriting the config file alone is not enough

Every existing install already passes `--kubelet-arg=config=/etc/rancher/k3s/kubelet-config.yaml`, so `imageMaximumGCAge` would apply if the file were rewritten. But the old k3s unit also carries `image-gc-high-threshold`, `image-gc-low-threshold` and a memory-only `eviction-hard` as CLI flags, and CLI flags beat config file fields. Rewriting only the file would keep the 85% threshold and drop the disk eviction signals. The systemd unit has to be regenerated too.

## Proposed solution

**Node side: make the installer idempotent against an existing node**

1. Detect an existing k3s install instead of failing or reinstalling.
2. Write the current kubelet config file, same content fresh installs get.
3. Rerun the k3s install script with `INSTALL_K3S_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true` and the current flag set. That regenerates the unit with the new flags and restarts k3s. A k3s restart does not restart workloads, containerd keeps the pods running.
4. Label the node with a config version, e.g. `unbind.app/node-config: 2`, bumped whenever the installer's node-level settings change.

This is the existing install path plus a detection branch and a label. Multi-node installs run it once per node.

**Product side: tell the user**

* The API lists nodes and compares the label to the version the running binary expects.
* Nodes with a missing or older label are surfaced on the update or system page as "this node needs a one-time host update", with the exact command to run.
* Fresh installs never see it. This also gives us a channel for any future node-level change.
* Optional verification instead of trusting the label: the kubelet `configz` endpoint via the node proxy exposes the live values, at the cost of a `nodes/proxy` get grant for the API service account.

## Options considered and rejected

* **Privileged DaemonSet shipped as a release manifest** that writes the file and calls `systemctl restart k3s` through nsenter. Zero user action, but it restarts the control plane while the update job is waiting on it, must also patch the unit file, and mutating the host from a pod is hard to make safe across distros. Multi-node makes it worse.
* **In-cluster prune job** that removes unused images through the containerd socket every few hours (`crictl rmi --prune` style). Duplicates kubelet GC, gives no eviction protection, and can race a fresh pull. Acceptable as a stopgap only.

## Going forward

The [UNB-259](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-259/old-container-imageslayer-snapshots-accumulate-on-nodes-and-fill-up) change moved every kubelet setting into the config file. Once nodes are on the regenerated unit, future tweaks only need the file rewritten plus a k3s restart. The one-time pain is the flags baked into old units.

## Same gap for BuildKit

The BuildKit changes from [UNB-259](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-259/old-container-imageslayer-snapshots-accumulate-on-nodes-and-fill-up) also only reach fresh installs:

* The GC bounds (`gc = true`, `reservedSpace`, `maxUsedSpace`, `minFreeSpace`) live in the `buildkit-config` ConfigMap, which the chart renders at install time. The API only rewrites that ConfigMap for `max-parallelism` and insecure registries, and `DefaultBuildkitConfig` is used only when the key is missing entirely. Existing installs keep BuildKit's default policy (60% of disk).
* The `--root /var/lib/buildkit` arg and the `maxSurge: 0` rollout strategy are chart-only deployment changes. Existing installs keep the cache in the container's writable layer, and a rollout of the `buildkit` deployment can deadlock on single-node installs because the default surge pod cannot schedule past the pod anti-affinity.

These need either a release manifest under `deploy/releases/<tag>/` that patches the ConfigMap and deployment, or a startup reconcile in the API that adds the GC lines and args when missing (the API already restarts buildkitd after ConfigMap changes). Unlike the kubelet part, this one can be fully automatic since it is all in-cluster.

Manual steps for the meantime:

```
kubectl -n unbind-system patch deployment buildkit --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/strategy","value":{"type":"RollingUpdate","rollingUpdate":{"maxSurge":0,"maxUnavailable":1}}},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--root"},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"/var/lib/buildkit"}
]'
kubectl -n unbind-system edit configmap buildkit-config   # add gc lines under [worker.oci]
kubectl -n unbind-system rollout restart deployment/buildkit
```

## Manual node steps for the kubelet part

Check disk first: the new config adds hard eviction at 15% free image space and 10% free node space, so a node already above 85% used evicts pods right after the restart. Run `k3s crictl rmi --prune` before restarting in that case.

```
# write /etc/rancher/k3s/kubelet-config.yaml with the content from apps/installer/internal/k3s/install.go (kubeletConfig const)
cp /etc/systemd/system/k3s.service /root/k3s.service.bak
sed -i -E "/--kubelet-arg=(eviction-soft|eviction-soft-grace-period|eviction-hard|eviction-minimum-reclaim|image-gc-high-threshold|image-gc-low-threshold)=/d" /etc/systemd/system/k3s.service
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart k3s
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$(hostname | tr A-Z a-z)/proxy/configz" | jq '.kubeletconfig | {imageGCHighThresholdPercent, imageGCLowThresholdPercent, imageMaximumGCAge, evictionHard}'
```

Agent nodes use `k3s-agent.service`. The old kubelet flags must be removed from the unit because CLI flags override config file fields.

issues.title: Database CPU tuning is hard-coded, and MySQL runs with crash safety off
issues.description:
The memory half of this issue was done in [UNB-318](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-318/figure-out-the-shared-buffers-situation-on-postgres-i-dont-think-we). This issue now tracks what is left.

## What remains

### 1. CPU tuning ignores the CPU limit

* **Postgres:** `max_parallel_workers` and `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` are pinned to 0, so parallel query is off at any size. Derive them from the CPU limit (for example workers = cores, per gather = cores / 2, capped at 4). Every parallel worker can use `work_mem` again, so check the memory math from [UNB-318](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-318/figure-out-the-shared-buffers-situation-on-postgres-i-dont-think-we) still holds before raising them. At the default 1 CPU limit nothing should change.
* **ClickHouse:** `config.d/99-low-resources.xml` pins `max_threads` to 1, so a 4 core ClickHouse runs every query on one thread. `max_block_size` 4096 and `max_download_threads` 1 are part of the same low resource profile. Derive `max_threads` from the CPU limit and revisit the rest of the profile for databases that have real resources.

Same rule as [UNB-318](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-318/figure-out-the-shared-buffers-situation-on-postgres-i-dont-think-we): with no CPU limit set, keep today's values. Never size from the whole server.

### 2. MySQL durability decision

`mysql/definition.yaml` sets `innodb_doublewrite: OFF`, `sync_binlog: 0` and `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit: 2`. A power loss or OOM kill can leave torn pages or lose the last second of commits, and users cannot see or change this. Decide: restore the safe defaults, or make it an explicit opt in.

### 3. Small MySQL leftovers

* `innodb_redo_log_capacity` is 64MB. It gets tight under heavy writes now that the buffer pool can be 1GB or more. It lives on the data volume, so it should follow the volume size, not memory. The operator already reads the real volume size for Postgres (`dataVolumeCapacity` in `apps/operator/internal/controller/database_volume.go`, works for MySQL claims too), reuse that and do not read the size recorded in the spec, it is frozen at creation.
* `table_open_cache` and `table_definition_cache` are 64. Apps with many tables will thrash.

## Done in [UNB-318](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-318/figure-out-the-shared-buffers-situation-on-postgres-i-dont-think-we)

Memory settings are now sized from the service's memory limit by one function in the operator (`apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/database_tuning.go`). With no memory limit nothing is set and the old values apply.

| Engine | Setting | Value |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Postgres | shared_buffers | 25% of the limit |
| Postgres | effective_cache_size | 75% of the limit |
| Postgres | maintenance_work_mem | 5%, floor 64MB, cap 1GB |
| Postgres | wal_buffers | shared_buffers / 32, floor 4MB, cap 16MB |
| Postgres | work_mem | (limit - shared_buffers) / (max_connections x 3), floor 4MB, cap 64MB |
| Postgres | max_wal_size | 10% of the real volume size, floor 256MB, cap 8GB |
| MySQL | innodb_buffer_pool_size | 50% of the limit, rounded down to whole chunks, instances pinned |
| MySQL | max_connections | limit MB / 20, floor 50, cap 1000 |
| MongoDB | wiredTigerCacheSizeGB | 50% of (limit - 1GB), floor 0.25 |
| MongoDB | maxConns | limit MB / 10, floor 100, cap 5000 |
| Redis | maxmemory | 75% of the limit, policy stays noeviction |

Two validated override fields on `DatabaseConfig`, available through the API and MCP (no UI yet): `sharedBuffersMb` (Postgres, at most 50% of the limit) and `innodbBufferPoolSizeMb` (MySQL, at most 75%). Lowering the memory limit under an existing override is rejected.

`max_wal_size` follows the real disk, not the size recorded in the spec (that one is frozen at creation, resizes land on the claims). The operator reads the smallest `status.capacity` of the database's claims and watches claims, so a resize is picked up about 20 seconds after the expansion finishes, with a config reload and no restart. Checked on the dev cluster: 1GB to 30GB to 50GB gave 256MB, 3GB, 5GB with the same Postgres start time.

Verified on the dev cluster for all four engines: values render, the databases restart on their own and pick them up, overrides apply and clear, and a limit change is followed.

## Suggestions from the original issue that were decided against

* **Derive in the template.** The template gets the limit as a string like `2048M`. Doing that math in Go templates is fragile and untestable, so it lives in the operator with table tests. The limit is decimal megabytes while Postgres and MySQL count in 1024 based units, so the function works in bytes.
* **Plumb the whole** `postgresql` **block through the API.** Free form strings with no validation make it easy to create a database that cannot boot. Two named, validated fields instead. More can be added the same way if someone needs them.
* **Scale max_wal_size with memory.** WAL lives on the data volume and default volumes are 1GB. It follows the volume size instead.
* **MySQL buffer pool at 50 to 70%.** 50%, because max_connections is raised at the same time and every connection has its own buffers. Also: MySQL 8.4 picks the buffer pool instance count from the host CPU count and rounds the pool up to 128MB x instances, so on a big server the pool lands well above the requested value. The instance count is now pinned from the pool size so the result is exact.
* **MongoDB: drop the cache flag.** Mongo sizes itself from the container limit, but with no limit it sizes from the whole server. Deriving the value keeps both cases safe.
* **Redis: evict by default.** People run queues and sessions on it. BullMQ and Sidekiq require noeviction, evicted keys silently corrupt a queue. Redis now rejects writes when full instead of being OOM killed, and keeps its data.
* **ClickHouse caches from the memory limit.** Not needed, ClickHouse caps its own memory from the container limit and the 500MB mark cache is only a ceiling.
* **Same sizing for Unbind's own database chart.** It is a small control plane database with a fixed 1GB limit. 128MB fits it, and changing it would restart Unbind's own database on upgrade for no real gain.

## Notes for whoever picks this up

* Values set with `ALTER SYSTEM` still win over what Unbind renders (checked on the dev cluster). `ALTER SYSTEM RESET <name>` plus a restart hands control back.
* Shipping [UNB-318](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-318/figure-out-the-shared-buffers-situation-on-postgres-i-dont-think-we) restarts every Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis that has a memory limit, once, on upgrade. CPU derived settings will do the same for databases whose values change, so try to ship them in one release.

issues.title: installer: Blacklist SCSI devices from multipathd on every node
issues.description:
## Problem

`multipathd` claims Longhorn's iSCSI block devices as multipath paths. When that happens the kubelet cannot mount the volume and the pod sits in `ContainerCreating` with:

```
MountVolume.MountDevice failed ... mount failed: exit status 32
/dev/longhorn/pvc-... already mounted or mount point busy.
```

`fuser -v /dev/sdX` shows `multipathd` holding the device and `multipath -ll` shows a map (for example `mpatha`) built on top of it.

This hit a real instance on 2026-09-11 after a ClickHouse volume was detached and reattached. `multipath-tools` is installed and enabled by default on Ubuntu Server, so any Unbind node is exposed. Longhorn's own installation requirements say to blacklist the devices.

## What to do

Have the installer configure multipathd on every node it sets up (server and agent), before Longhorn is installed:

* Ensure `/etc/multipath.conf` has a blacklist for plain SCSI devices:

```
blacklist {
    devnode "^sd[a-z0-9]+"
}
```

* If the file already has a `blacklist` section, add the `devnode` line inside it instead of appending a second section.
* Restart `multipathd` if it is running. Skip everything quietly if `multipath-tools` is not installed.

The add-node command printed by the management script should apply the same change.

## Manual fix on an affected node

```
cat >> /etc/multipath.conf <<'EOF'

blacklist {
    devnode "^sd[a-z0-9]+"
}
EOF
multipath -f <map name from multipath -ll>
systemctl restart multipathd
```

The kubelet retries the mount on its own afterwards.

## Reference

[https://longhorn.io/kb/troubleshooting-volume-with-multipath/](<https://longhorn.io/kb/troubleshooting-volume-with-multipath/>)

issues.title: GitHub apps are system-level in the DB but per-user in the API and team-level in the UI
issues.description:
GitHub apps have three different scopes depending on where you look, and none of them agree.

## Current state

**Schema — system-level.** `GithubApp` (`apps/api/ent/schema/github_app.go`) has two edges: O2M to `GithubInstallation`, and M2O to `User` via `created_by`. No team edge. `GithubInstallation` links to its app and to services. Nothing associates either with a team.

**API — inconsistent, per-user where it matters.**

* `GET /github/apps` → `GetApps()` returns every app in the install, no filter, no permission check beyond being authenticated (`internal/api/handlers/github/apps.go:172`).
* `GET /github/installations` and `GET /github/repositories` → both call `GetInstallationsByCreator(ctx, user.ID)`, each with a `// ! TODO - RBAC` comment. That repo method filters on the **app's** `created_by`, not the installation's, so when two users install the same app both installations are visible only to whoever created the app.

**UI — team-level by URL only.** The flow is `/$team_id/connect-git/connected/github` and the command panel builds the redirect from `teamId` (`apps/web/src/components/command-panel/context-command-panel/items/git.tsx:165`). The team id only routes the user back; nothing team-scoped is persisted.

## What this produces

* A service in any team can reference any installation. Nothing validates installation-against-team at service creation; redeploy just looks it up by ID (`internal/services/service/redeploy.go:36`).
* Two admins on the same team can't see each other's connected repos in the repo picker.
* If the admin who connected GitHub is deleted, the app rows survive but the repos vanish from everyone's picker, with no way to recover them from the UI.
* `list-apps` exposes the name and creator of every GitHub app to any authenticated user, including non-admins.

## Decision to make

Pick one scope and make all three layers agree.

**Option A — system-level (recommended).** Drop the creator filter, gate the three read endpoints on the existing `system` resource permission (view for reads, edit for connecting), and manage apps and installations from system settings. Keep the per-team connect entry point as a shortcut into it. Fits a self-hosted install where an admin connects the org's GitHub once.

**Option B — actually team-scoped.** Add a team edge to `GithubApp`, filter by team permission, validate installation-against-team at service creation, keep the UI where it is. More work, and buys little for the common self-hosted case.

Either way the `! TODO - RBAC` comments go away and `list-apps` stops being readable by non-admins.

Related: [UNB-300](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-300/improve-systemsettings) (improve system/settings) — a "Git" tab there only makes sense after this is settled, since the creator filter would otherwise show different repos to different admins.

issues.title: Bugs in the /system settings and domain endpoints
issues.description:
Found while reading the system handlers for [UNB-300](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-300/improve-systemsettings). All five are in `apps/api/internal/api/handlers/system/` or the service layer behind it. Independent of each other, roughly in severity order.

## 1. `check-unique-domain` is dead — always 400

`CheckUniqueDomainInput.domain` is unexported (`handlers/system/domain.go:73`), so huma never binds it. It's not just empty at runtime: huma drops the field from the spec entirely, and the generated web client signature is `check: async (params?: undefined, ...)` (`apps/web/src/lib/server/client.gen.ts:7266`) — the endpoint takes no input at all.

Every call then runs `CleanAndValidateHost("")`, which fails the "must contain at least one dot" check and returns `400 Invalid domain`. `GET /system/domain/check` has never worked.

Fix: export the field (`Domain string \`query:"domain"``) and update the reference in the handler body. Worth a test that actually exercises the route, since the type system won't catch this class of bug.

## 2. `registry_cache_settings` is accepted and silently dropped

`SystemSettingUpdateInput` includes `RegistryCacheSettings` (`repositories/system/settings.go:25`) and `PUT /system/settings/update` accepts it, but `SystemService.UpdateSettings` builds a fresh input containing only `WildcardDomain` and `BuildkitSettings` when it calls the repo (`services/system/read_settings.go`). The repo's `SetRegistryCacheSettings` branch is unreachable from HTTP.

The write returns 200 and does nothing. Fix: either forward the field, or drop it from the input struct and leave `/system/cache/registry/update` as the only way in.

## 3. `can_update_buildkit` is always false in the update response

`GetSettings` computes `CanUpdateBuildkit` from `buildkitManager.GetBuildkitConfig`, but `UpdateSettings` constructs its `SystemSettingsResponse` without the field, so `PUT /system/settings/update` always returns `can_update_buildkit: false`. Any client trusting the response body would conclude Buildkit is externally managed and disable the form. The web only escapes it because the form refetches after saving.

## 4. The wildcard domain can't be cleared

`UpdateSystemSettings` has a `ClearWildcardBaseURL` branch for an empty string, but the handler DNS-validates whatever is sent first. With `""`: `IsPointingToIP("", ...)` fails its lookup and returns `(false, nil)` for both v4 and v6, then `IsUsingCloudflareProxy("")` returns an error — so the request ends as `500 Error checking Cloudflare` (`handlers/system/settings.go`). The clear branch is unreachable.

Fix: guard the empty case before the DNS checks and skip straight to the update.

## 5. `UpdateBuildkitSettings` is misnamed

The handler bound to `PUT /system/settings/update` handles all system settings, not just Buildkit (`handlers/system/settings.go:27`). Several log lines below it also say "buildkit settings" while operating on the whole settings object. Rename for readability.

issues.title: Editing DATABASE_PASSWORD silently breaks every connection string
issues.description:
Nobody owns the database credential. The UI, the operator and the API sync cron all write it, and the guards between them are wrong in both directions: a user can change it and break everything, while a real rotation in the engine never reaches us.

## Changing it in the UI

The padlock on `DATABASE_PASSWORD` is decorative. `protected_variables` filters `deletes` but not `upserts` in `write.go`, so the edit goes through. Then:

1. The database service redeploys, and so does everything referencing it.
2. The operator skips restoring the real value — `syncCredentialSecret` sees `DATABASE_USERNAME`, `DATABASE_PASSWORD` and `DATABASE_URL` already present and logs "Target secret already has credentials, skipping copy".
3. Within 10 minutes the API cron reads the wrong password, sees it is non-empty so does not re-fetch from the engine's secret, and rebuilds `DATABASE_URL` around it.
4. The actual password in the engine never changed.

Every connection string in the environment is now wrong, apps restart with them, and nothing reports an error. The only recovery is deleting the key, which is the one operation protection does block.

## Rotating it in the engine

Same guard, opposite direction. `hasDatabaseCredentials` is first-write-wins, so once the keys exist the operator never copies again. A password rotated in Zalando, MOCO or the MongoDB secret stays invisible to Unbind forever.

## Redis is different

The Redis chart reads `existingSecretPasswordKey: DATABASE_PASSWORD` from our secret, so there Unbind genuinely owns the credential and editing it is legitimate — it takes effect on the next rollout.

## Fix: one owner per credential

* **Engine-owned** (postgres, mysql, mongodb, clickhouse): reject upserts of protected keys in `write.go`, and drop the `hasDatabaseCredentials` guard so the operator overwrites unconditionally. The engine is the source of truth in both directions.
* **Unbind-owned** (redis): stays editable, operator never touches it.

Rejecting protected upserts also makes the padlock mean what it looks like it means, for every protected key rather than just this one.

## Files

* `apps/api/internal/services/variables/write.go` — protected keys filtered from deletes only
* `apps/operator/internal/controller/credentials.go` — `hasDatabaseCredentials` / `syncCredentialSecret`
* `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/database_secrets.go` — cron rebuilds the URL from whatever it finds

Related to the database URL work in [UNB-190](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-190/figure-out-the-database-public-url-situation): once the URLs are computed rather than stored, they cannot drift from the credential, but the ownership question here is separate and worth fixing on its own.

issues.title: api: Cache Kubernetes reads instead of re-listing on every poll
issues.description:
The UI polls several endpoints per open tab (`/replicas/health` every 3s, `/volumes`, `/deployments`, `/replicas`, `/services/endpoints/list` every 5s). issues.title: Improve new project button on the projects page
Builder passes raw ${{...}} templates instead of rendered values for referenced variables
issues.description:
## Problem

Variables that reference other services (e.g. `API_URL=${{service.<id>.HTTP}}`) reach the **build** with the raw template string instead of the rendered value. At runtime the pod gets the rendered value, so the app works once deployed, but anything that reads the variable during the build sees `${{service....}}`.

Concrete case: bambu-dashboard web service. `API_URL` references the API service. The TanStack Start build prerenders pages and validates env with `@t3-oss/env-core` (`z.url()`), which fails during the build:

```
❌ Invalid environment variables: [
  { code: 'invalid_format', format: 'url', path: [ 'API_URL' ], message: 'Invalid URL' }
]
```

## Root cause

`apps/api/cmd/builder/main.go` merges the two variable sources in the wrong order:

1. `ADDITIONAL_ENV` (rendered references from `RenderServiceVariables`) is decoded into `buildSecrets` first.
2. `SERVICE_BUILD_SECRETS` (the raw Kubernetes secret map, which still holds the template strings) is decoded **after** and overwrites the rendered entries with the raw templates.

`deployctl.go` sets `SERVICE_BUILD_SECRETS` from `GetSecretMap` (raw) and `ADDITIONAL_ENV` from `RenderServiceVariables` (rendered). Runtime is unaffected because `DeployImage` receives `additionalEnv` (rendered) separately.

## Fix

Apply the raw secret map first, then overlay the rendered references so rendered values win. Same ordering issue should be checked for the Dockerfile builder path since it uses the same `buildSecrets` map.

## Repro

1. Create service B with a variable `API_URL=${{service.<A id>.HTTP}}`.
2. Add a build step that prints or validates `API_URL` (e.g. `echo $API_URL` in the build command).
3. Build: the output is the literal template, not the URL.

issues.title: OAuth authorization server and Connected Apps for MCP clients
issues.description:
## Why

The MCP server ([UNB-296](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-296/create-an-mcp-server)) has to work with clients that only speak OAuth: [claude.ai](<http://claude.ai>) and ChatGPT connectors cannot send a static `Authorization: Bearer unb_...` header. Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Codex) also prefer OAuth when the server offers it. API keys stay as the option for scripts and CI.

Today Unbind is not an authorization server. `/auth/login` issues a session, `oauth2_tokens` stores session refresh tokens, and the OIDC discovery + JWKS endpoints exist only so Kubernetes can verify our JWTs. `oauth2_codes` and its repository are unused leftovers.

## What to build

The MCP authorization profile (OAuth 2.1), kept to the narrow subset MCP needs:

**api**

* Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, and `/mcp` answers 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="..."`.
* Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414).
* Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591). Public clients only, no client secrets. Decide whether to also accept Client ID Metadata Documents (newer MCP spec revision). It needs the server to fetch a client supplied URL, so it needs SSRF protection if we do it.
* `/authorize` and `/token`: authorization code with PKCE (S256 required), `resource` parameter (RFC 8707) so tokens are bound to this instance's MCP URL, refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection.
* Tokens are opaque and stored hashed, same approach as API keys (`internal/auth/apikey.go`), with their own prefix so the auth middleware can tell them apart. Short lived access token (about 1 hour) plus rotating refresh token. Opaque rather than JWT so a revoke takes effect immediately.
* A grant carries the same access model as an API key: role (read only or read/write) plus full access or a list of teams / projects / environments / services. Reuse `permissions_repo.APIKeyAccess` so permission narrowing has a single code path. The grant can never exceed the user's own permissions, same as keys.
* OAuth tokens get the same treatment as API keys in `middleware.Authenticate`: refused on session only routes, no Kubernetes identity, writes blocked for read only grants, last used tracking.
* Endpoints to list and revoke the current user's grants (session only). Revoking kills the access and refresh tokens at once. Deleting a user removes their grants.

**web**

* Consent page at the authorize step: user must be signed in (redirect through `/sign-in` and back), sees the client name and redirect host, picks role and resources with the same components as the API key form, then approves or denies. The client name is self reported through registration, so the page has to show it as unverified and show where it redirects to.
* "Connected Apps" tab in account settings next to "API Keys": client name, access, connected date, last used, revoke. Same card and timeline patterns as the API keys page.

## Security requirements

* Redirect URIs: exact match only. Allow https, and http only for loopback (native clients).
* Authorization codes: single use, about 60 seconds, stored hashed, bound to client, redirect URI, PKCE challenge and resource.
* Consent approval is a session + CSRF protected POST. Consent page sends `frame-ancestors 'none'`.
* Registration is unauthenticated by design, so rate limit it, cap field sizes, and clean up clients that never completed a grant.
* Token endpoint and registration are rate limited.
* Never accept tokens whose audience is not this instance's MCP resource. For now OAuth tokens are only valid for `/mcp` (and whatever the MCP tools call in process), not as a general REST API credential. Revisit later if needed.

## Decisions to make before starting

1. Library or hand written. Candidates: `ory/fosite` (battle tested, heavy, no dynamic registration, needs a lot of storage glue) or a hand written narrow profile (public clients, S256 only, code + refresh grants only). The MCP Go SDK (`modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk`) already ships the resource server side helpers (bearer middleware, protected resource metadata handler).
2. Issuer and metadata location. The existing issuer is `<host>/api/oauth2`. The web ingress already sends `/` to the API, so root level `/.well-known/oauth-*`, `/mcp`, `/oauth/*` reach the API with no chart change. Confirm the same is true for the Gateway API routes.
3. Whether system admins need a view of all registered clients and grants across users. Suggest not in the first version.
4. Drop or reuse the unused `oauth2_codes` table.

## Out of scope

* Unbind as a general OAuth / OIDC provider for third party apps.
* Confidential clients, client credentials grant, device flow.

issues.title: S3 bucket read endpoints return the secret key in plaintext to any team viewer
issues.description:
## Problem

`GET /storage/s3/list` and `GET /storage/s3/get` return each bucket's `access_key` and `secret_key` in plaintext. The only permission check is team viewer, so anyone who can see a team can read the credentials of every S3 bucket stored for it. Read only API keys get them too, because both endpoints are plain `Read` operations.

Found while working on [UNB-296](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-296/create-an-mcp-server) by reading the code. The endpoints were not called to confirm it live.

## Where

* `apps/api/internal/services/storage/s3_read.go`: `GetS3BucketByID` and `ListS3Buckets` check `ActionViewer` on the team, then read the Kubernetes secret and pass both keys into the response.
* `apps/api/internal/models/s3_bucket_response.go`: `S3BucketResponse` has `access_key` and `secret_key` fields.
* `s3_create.go` and `s3_update.go` also echo the credentials back in their responses.

## Why it matters

* A viewer role is meant to be read only, but with the bucket credentials a viewer can read, overwrite or delete the backups in that bucket outside of Unbind.
* A leaked read only API key leaks the S3 credentials with it.

## Who reads these fields today

* `apps/web/src/components/storage/s3-bucket-card.tsx` shows `access_key` as "Access Key ID" and uses `access_key` plus `secret_key` to prefill the edit form (lines 182 to 183 and 234).
* Nothing else in the web app reads them.

## Suggested fix

* Never return `secret_key` from any S3 endpoint. Treat it as write only, the same way the update input already lets it be omitted to keep the current value.
* Keep returning `access_key` (it is an identifier, not a secret), or gate it behind editor if we want to be strict.
* Web: stop prefilling the secret in the edit form. Leave the field empty with a "leave blank to keep the current secret" hint, which `S3BucketUpdateInput` already supports.
* Add a test that the list and get responses carry no secret.

## MCP

All six S3 endpoints are opted out of the MCP server with `oapi.NoMCP` for this reason. Once the responses no longer carry the secret, `list-s3-buckets` and `get-s3-bucket-by-id` can be switched to `oapi.MCP`, so an agent can pick a backup target by ID.

issues.title: TLS for public database connections
issues.description:
Public database connections are not encrypted today. Anyone who connects with the public URL sends the password and all data over the internet in plain text.

## Where it comes from

* The generated connection strings turn TLS off: `?sslmode=disable` for Postgres and `?ssl=false` for MongoDB (`apps/api/pkg/databases/connstring.go`). The ClickHouse HTTP string is plain `http://`.
* Public exposure is raw L4. The operator builds a `<name>-db` NodePort service, or a Gateway TCPRoute on gateway clusters, and no certificate is issued for it. Endpoint discovery reports these as `tls_status: not_available`.
* The `CapTLS` (SNI passthrough) provider capability exists but databases do not use it.
* Databases are private by default since 2026-09-21 (`resolveIsPublic` in `apps/api/internal/services/service/create.go`), so only a database switched to Public has a plaintext public URL.

## Why now

The Connect card ([UNB-315](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-315/connect-card-for-dbs)) puts the public URL in front of users right after launch. It labels the private connection as recommended and warns that the public one is not encrypted, but that is a label, not a fix.

## To decide

* Turn TLS on in each engine (Zalando Postgres, MOCO, the MongoDB, Redis and ClickHouse charts) with a cert-manager certificate, then drop `sslmode=disable` / `ssl=false` from the public strings. The private strings can stay as they are.
* Or terminate or pass through TLS at the gateway for the engines that support it.

Webhooks fire across teams and only the first one is delivered
issues.description:
Found while documenting webhooks for [UNB-327](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-327/docs-site). Two bugs in the same function, one of them a data leak between teams.

## Problem

**1. Webhooks are not scoped to their team or project.**
`GetWebhooksForEvent` in `apps/api/internal/repositories/webhook/queries.go` filters on the event only. Webhook rows have `team_id` and an optional `project_id`, but the lookup ignores both. A webhook in team A receives events from every other team and project on the instance, including service names and URLs.

**2. Only the first matching webhook is delivered.**
In `TriggerWebhooks` (`apps/api/internal/services/webooks/trigger.go`) the Discord, Slack and Telegram branches `return` inside the loop. When several webhooks subscribe to the same event, only the newest one is sent. The generic branch also returns on the first error, so one broken URL blocks every webhook after it.

## Fix

* Give `TriggerWebhooks` the team ID and the project ID.
  * Project events (`project.*`) look up team webhooks of that team.
  * Service and deployment events look up webhooks of that project.
* Update the 8 call sites: `project/create|update|delete`, `service/create|update|delete`, and two in `deployctl`.
* Send to every matching webhook. When one fails, log it and carry on.

## Tests

* A webhook in team A gets nothing from team B.
* A webhook in project A gets nothing from project B of the same team.
* Two webhooks on the same event both receive it.
* One failing URL does not stop the next.

## Notes

* Own commit, and it should go out in a release soon since it leaks data between teams.
* Docs: `apps/docs/content/(platform)/monitoring/webhooks.mdx` needs no change, it already describes the intended behavior.

## Problem

Calling `create-service` with `repository_owner: unbindapp`, `repository_name: unbind` and the installation of the personal `yekta` account created a service pointing at `yekta/unbind`, an unrelated repo. No error, no warning.

Why, in `apps/api/internal/services/service/create.go`:

1. `VerifyRepositoryAccess` calls GitHub's "get repository" with the installation token. That succeeds for any **public** repo with any installation token, so the check passed for `unbindapp/unbind`.
2. The code then sets the stored owner to `installation.AccountLogin` instead of the owner that was asked for, which turned it into `yekta/unbind`.

## Fix

* In `VerifyRepositoryAccess` (`apps/api/internal/integrations/github/repositories.go`), require that the repo's owner equals the installation's account, compared case-insensitively. Otherwise answer "Repository not accessible with the specified GitHub installation".
* Store the owner GitHub returned, not the installation's login.
* Check whether `update-service` or any other path repeats the pattern.

Rejecting is correct even for public repos: a repo outside the installation never sends push events, so auto-deploy would silently never work.

## Tests

* Owner mismatch is rejected.
* Matching owner with different letter case passes.

  * Ghost: `/var/lib/ghost/content`
  * WordPress: `/var/www/html`
* Ghost runs as a non-root user and a fresh volume is owned by root. It probably needs the same ownership-fixing init container Flowise uses. Confirm on the dev box.
* Bump both template versions.
* Run `./scripts/gen-docs-data.sh` and remove the two warning callouts from `apps/docs/content/(platform)/templates/ghost.mdx` and `wordpress.mdx`.

## Testing

On the dev box, one template at a time: deploy, upload an image, redeploy, check that the image is still there.

## Limitation

Templates are immutable per version, so existing Ghost and WordPress deployments are not upgraded. The release notes should tell those users to add a volume by hand, and the docs pages should keep a short note for people who deployed before the fix.

issues.title: Sticky session cookie is set on every service and blocks Cloudflare caching
issues.description:
## Problem

The operator enables cookie session affinity on every service with a public host. Nginx, Traefik and Envoy Gateway all set a `<service>-session` cookie on every response, including hashed static assets.

Cloudflare refuses to cache any response that carries `Set-Cookie`. On [docs.unbind.app](<http://docs.unbind.app>) the assets under `/assets/*` are served with `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and still come back `cf-cache-status: BYPASS`. The HTML is `DYNAMIC`. Nothing is cached. Any Unbind service behind Cloudflare (or any CDN with the same rule) has the same problem.

## Where it comes from

* `apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/nginx.go` (`nginxAnnotations`, `affinity: cookie`)
* `apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/traefik.go` (`service.sticky.cookie`)
* `apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/gateway.go` (`envoyAffinityPolicy`, ConsistentHash on cookie)

The cookie is unconditional. The builder already has `Service.Spec.Config.Replicas`, so replica count is available at the point where the annotations are built.

## Proposal

1. Only apply cookie affinity when the service has more than one replica. A single replica has nothing to be sticky to, so the cookie is pure cost.
2. Add a per-service toggle in the service config (API + CRD + UI) so users can turn stickiness off on multi-replica stateless services and turn it on where they need it. Default: on for more than one replica, off for one.
3. Cover all three providers so behaviour matches regardless of the ingress controller.

## Verification

```
curl -sI https://docs.unbind.app/assets/<hash>.css | grep -iE 'cf-cache-status|set-cookie'
```

Should show no `set-cookie` and `cf-cache-status: HIT` on the second request.

comments.body:
Closing, the premise was wrong. The proxy only sets the cookie on requests that don't already carry it. Browsers get it from the HTML response before fetching assets, so asset requests carry it, get no `set-cookie` and are cached. After that, every visitor, with or without the cookie, gets `HIT`.

Tested on docs.unbind.app:

* No cookie, asset never requested with one: `BYPASS` + `set-cookie`
* With the cookie: `MISS`, no `set-cookie`
* No cookie, after that: `HIT`

The cost is one extra fetch from the service per asset per Cloudflare location. `DYNAMIC` on the HTML is Cloudflare's default for HTML, not the cookie.

Sticky sessions stay on as they are. Template apps with in-memory sessions, Socket.IO long-polling or chunked uploads need them when scaled up.

issues.title: Domains behind Cloudflare fail in SSL Full (strict) mode
issues.description:
Split out of [UNB-343](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-343/for-service-i-cant-seem-to-be-delete-the-first-public-networking-item). Public domains proxied through Cloudflare can fail when the zone is in SSL "Full (strict)" mode.

## What happens

Every service host gets its own Let's Encrypt certificate over HTTP-01, from the single `letsencrypt-prod` ClusterIssuer (`deploy/charts/helmfile.yaml.gotmpl:703-726`). Until that certificate exists the origin serves an untrusted one:

* gateway: cert-manager's temporary self-signed certificate (`apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/gateway.go:217`)
* nginx: the ingress controller's fake certificate
* traefik: the default certificate

Full (strict) rejects all of these with a 526, while plain Full accepts them. That matches the report that only strict mode fails.

If the zone redirects HTTP to HTTPS ("Always Use HTTPS", HSTS or a redirect rule), the ACME challenge can also end up on the untrusted origin certificate. The certificate then never issues and the site stays on 526. With the gateway provider, a challenge that arrives over HTTPS can't reach the solver at all: the solver route is only attached to the shared gateway's :80 listener, and service gateways have no :80 listener.

## Why the UI doesn't show it

* `reachableThroughCloudflare` (`apps/api/internal/infrastructure/k8s/dns_discovery.go:346-358`) counts any HTTP response as reachable, including a Cloudflare 525/526 page.
* `ServesTLS` (`apps/api/internal/common/utils/dnscheck.go:53-62`) uses `InsecureSkipVerify` against Cloudflare's edge, not the origin.
* `cloudflare_missing_certificate` is in the API response, but the web app doesn't use it.

## Related: deep wildcards

A generated domain like `x.unbind.yekta.cc` is two levels below the zone. Cloudflare's free Universal SSL only covers `*.yekta.cc`, so proxied generated domains under a deep wildcard have no edge certificate in any SSL mode. The installer warns about this, but the wildcard domain settings in the app don't.

## Fix options

1. **DNS-01 with a Cloudflare API token** as a second issuer, chosen for Cloudflare-proxied hosts. Works in every proxy mode and allows a real wildcard certificate for the wildcard domain.
2. **Cloudflare Origin CA** (cert-manager `origin-ca-issuer`) for proxied hosts.
3. **Make HTTP-01 survive redirects on gateway clusters**: make the solver reachable for the host on :443, and add a :80 listener that redirects to HTTPS except for `/.well-known/acme-challenge/`.
4. **Surface the failure**: treat 525/526 and untrusted origin certificates as failures in the status checks, show `cloudflare_missing_certificate`, show failed cert-manager Challenge reasons, and add a hint in the UI ("Full (strict) needs a valid origin certificate").

## Needed to reproduce

The failing host, the Cloudflare error code (525 or 526), whether the record is proxied, and whether "Always Use HTTPS" is on.

comments.body:
UNB-407 overlaps fix option 3 here (a :80 listener that redirects to HTTPS except ACME challenges). It was filed from banano, where plain HTTP to a service domain gets 404 `NR`.

On banano (Cloudflare Full), moving a domain between services gave 8 to 13 s of 404, 503 or 525 per domain.
