issues.title: Single instance services: never run the old and new replica at the same time
issues.description:
Services without a volume deploy with a rolling update (`buildDeploymentStrategy` in `apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/deployment.go`). With 1 replica that means max surge 1: every redeploy starts the new pod next to the old one and stops the old one once the new one is ready. Only services with a volume get `Recreate`.

For some apps two copies must never run, even for a few seconds.

**Seen on banano**

* wban-api (5 bridges). Each holds a Banano seed and a chain mnemonic for its hot wallets. Adding the domains on 2026-10-14 redeployed all five, and each had about 30 s with two pods on the same wallets. BullMQ job ids and locks probably prevent double sends, but that was not checked.
* graham Discord bots: two pods would run the same bot token at once. (pippin takes a Redis lock per wallet and account, so overlap there is guarded.)
* Workaround today: auto deploy off on wban-api, and a script (`new-unbind/wban-deploy.sh`) that stops the service, deploys at 0 replicas, then starts it. Any change that redeploys (domains, variables) still overlaps.

**After the change**

A per-service "Single instance" setting renders `strategy: Recreate`, so a redeploy stops the old pod before the new one starts. A few seconds of downtime instead of overlap. wban-api could go back to auto deploy.

**Proposal**

Service setting `single_instance` (API, MCP, settings UI), only for 1 replica. Forces `Recreate`. Rolling stays the default.

issues.title: Cron services get a detected port and a public domain
issues.description:
Creating a git service with `cron_schedule` still detects the Dockerfile's `EXPOSE`, adds that port, turns `is_public` on and adds a `<name>.apps.<wildcard domain>` host (`addDetectedPorts` in `apps/api/internal/services/service/create.go`). A cron run has no long-running replicas, so nothing answers on that domain.

**Seen on banano**

* kalium-prices: got port 3000 and a public host, removed by hand.
* wban polygon `bc-scan-failed-cleaner` (built from wban-backend, which has `EXPOSE 3000`): got port 3000 and `bc-scan-failed-cleaner-ec7rwr9evwx7.apps.banano.cc`, removed by hand.
* natrium-prices got only the port because `is_public: false` was passed on create.

**After the change**

Cron services are created without detected ports and hosts. No stray public domains (and certificates) for jobs.

**Proposal**

Skip port detection and the generated domain when `cron_schedule` is set, on create and when an existing service switches to a schedule. Possibly refuse hosts on cron services the same way replicas and ports are refused.

issues.title: update-service: empty overwrite_hosts / overwrite_ports are ignored, and is_public false is dropped
issues.description:
`overwrite_hosts: []` and `overwrite_ports: []` do nothing, because the repository only applies them when `len(...) > 0` (`apps/api/internal/repositories/service/mutations.go` around lines 230 and 541). There is no way to say "replace with nothing". `is_public: false` in the same request is also dropped while the service still has a host, so the request answers 200 with everything unchanged.

**Seen on banano**

Clearing the stray domain on the wban `bc-scan-failed-cleaner` cron (2026-10-14). `overwrite_hosts: []`, `overwrite_ports: []`, `is_public: false` returned the service unchanged. `remove_hosts` with the exact host plus `remove_ports` plus `is_public: false` worked.

**After the change**

An empty overwrite list clears the field, and `is_public: false` applies (or the request fails with a clear error instead of silently ignoring it). MCP clients can clear a service's domains in one call without knowing them.

**Proposal**

Treat a present but empty `overwrite_*` list as "set to empty" (distinguish nil from empty in the input structs), and apply `is_public` after hosts are resolved. Add humatest cases for both.

issues.title: Postgres credentials are copied into the service Secret once and never reconciled
issues.description:
The operator copies the Postgres operator's credentials secret (`<role>.<cluster>.credentials.postgresql.acid.zalan.do`) into the database service's Secret only while the service Secret has no `DATABASE_PASSWORD` (`apps/operator/internal/controller/credentials.go`). If the Postgres operator's secret is ever recreated, it generates a new password it cannot apply to the existing role, and the role, the operator secret and the service Secret drift apart. Nothing reconciles them. Apps keep working until their next restart, then fail with `28P01`.

**Seen on banano**

v0.1.101 deleted those secrets during route cleanup (fixed in v0.1.102). Recovery took `ALTER ROLE` by hand for 18 roles across 6 clusters (`new-unbind/realign-pg-passwords.sh`), plus removing `DATABASE_PASSWORD` from one service Secret so the operator copied it again. Synapse needed its homeserver config script rerun because it bakes the password in.

**After the change**

The service Secret, the operator secret and the role password stay in sync on their own. A lost or recreated operator secret heals without manual SQL, and apps that reference `DATABASE_PASSWORD` roll out with the right value.

**Proposal**

Treat the service Secret as the source of truth after the first copy: when the operator secret differs, write the service's password back into it and run `ALTER ROLE` (or let the Postgres operator do it through its password rotation hooks). Alert if they cannot be reconciled.

issues.title: Redis backups to S3
issues.description:
Redis is the only database without backups (the Backups section was removed in [UNB-335](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-335/redis-shows-a-backups-section-it-cannot-use) because it never worked). With the append-only file from [UNB-399](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-399/redis-append-only-file-on-by-default-for-new-databases) a crash loses at most a second, but the data still lives on one volume with no off-site copy.

**Seen on banano**

* wBAN keeps user balances, deposits, withdrawals, swaps and claims in Redis, one database per chain (bsc 180k keys, arbitrum 51k, ethereum 47k, fantom 47k, polygon 35k). Losing a volume loses the bridge's accounting.
* boompow keeps client scores (`clientscores`) and service tokens (`servicetokens`) only in Redis.

**After the change**

Redis gets the same backup schedule, retention and S3 bucket choice as the other databases. A lost volume can be restored from the bucket.

**Proposal**

Scheduled `BGSAVE` (or `redis-cli --rdb`) uploaded to the backup bucket, same settings as Postgres/MySQL. Restore by placing the RDB on the volume with the AOF conversion init container from [UNB-399](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-399/redis-append-only-file-on-by-default-for-new-databases) (it already turns an RDB into an AOF on start).

issues.title: Gateway provider: no way to expose a TCP port to a few outside hosts only
issues.description:
With the gateway provider a port's `node_port` becomes a listener on the public load balancer (the operator skips the NodePort Service when routing through the gateway). Hetzner firewalls do not apply to load balancers, so the port is open to the whole internet.

**Seen on banano**

The banano and nano nodes post block callbacks to betsy from outside the cluster. Betsy got hand-made NodePort Services (`betsy-banano-callbacks` 30756, `betsy-nano-callbacks` 30755) plus a `firewall_extra_rules` entry in terraform for the two node IPs. These live outside Unbind, so Unbind does not know about them and a redeploy or rename can break them silently.

**After the change**

A port can be exposed as a plain NodePort (node firewall applies) or as a load balancer listener with a source IP allowlist. Betsy's callbacks become normal Unbind config and the hand-made Services go away. Related: [UNB-376](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-376/banano-move-banano-node-and-nano-node-into-the-new-project-network) (moving the nodes onto the cluster network would also remove the need here).

**Proposal**

Per-port choice: load balancer (today) or NodePort. Optionally `allowed_sources` on L4 listeners via an Envoy Gateway `SecurityPolicy` / `ClientTrafficPolicy`.

issues.title: Envoy settings are not configurable (replicas, spread, PDB, load balancer annotations)
issues.description:
The EnvoyProxy is written by a postsync `kubectl apply` hook with only `mergeGateways`, so chart values cannot change it. Envoy runs 1 replica, and its Service uses `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, so on a multi-node cluster the load balancer has one healthy target and Envoy is a single point of failure. There is no way to set load balancer annotations either.

**Seen on banano**

* Patched by hand to 3 replicas with topology spread (`matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]`) and a PDB (maxUnavailable 1). The next chart upgrade can overwrite it.
* With `Local`, every node without an Envoy pod fails the load balancer health check. After adding a 4th node (worker) the Hetzner LB showed 6/8 checks passing. Fixed by labelling the worker `node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers=true` (and in terraform).

**After the change**

Replicas, spread, PDB and service annotations come from values and survive upgrades. Clusters with dedicated worker nodes can keep the LB targets to the nodes that run Envoy, or run Envoy on every node.

**Proposal**

Values for replicas (or a DaemonSet mode), topology spread, PDB, node selector, and service annotations, rendered into the EnvoyProxy instead of the hook's fixed spec. Document the exclude label for nodes that should not take LB traffic.

issues.title: Gateway provider: plain HTTP to a service domain returns 404 instead of redirecting
issues.description:
On the gateway provider, port 80 only answers ACME challenges. Any other plain HTTP request to a service domain gets 404 with Envoy flag `NR` (no route). There is no HTTP to HTTPS redirect.

**Seen on banano**

* The old cluster's cert-manager kept retrying HTTP-01 for migrated hosts ([natrium.io](<http://natrium.io>) among them), and the Envoy access log shows those requests answered 404 `NR` on port 80.
* Any visitor typing `http://` on a domain that is not proxied through Cloudflare gets a 404.
* A Cloudflare zone in Flexible SSL mode would get 404 for every request. The migration notes had to call out Full as a requirement for every zone.

**After the change**

`http://` requests to a service domain get a 301/308 to `https://`, ACME challenges keep working.

**Proposal**

A redirect route on the port 80 listener for every service domain (HTTPRoute with `RequestRedirect` scheme https), keeping the ACME solver routes more specific. Or document that Cloudflare must use Full / Full (strict) and that DNS-only domains have no HTTP. Related: [UNB-344](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-344/domains-behind-cloudflare-fail-in-ssl-full-strict-mode).

issues.title: Pod Security labels on unbind-system and team namespaces for non-k3s clusters
issues.description:
helmfile creates `unbind-system` without Pod Security labels, and team namespaces are created without them too. Distros that enforce `baseline` by default reject the platform's own pods.

**Seen on banano (Talos)**

buildkit (privileged), alloy (hostPath) and node-exporter (host network) were rejected in `unbind-system`. Worked around by creating `unbind-system` by hand with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged` before the install.

**After the change**

Unbind installs on Talos and other hardened distros without pre-creating namespaces. Team namespaces get an explicit level, so a service that asks for privileges fails with a clear error instead of a rejected pod.

**Proposal**

Label `unbind-system` `enforce: privileged` in the chart. Decide the level for team namespaces (probably `baseline`, raised per service that needs more) and label them when the API creates them.

issues.title: Docs: bring your own cluster requirements beyond k3s (Talos on Hetzner as the example)
issues.description:
The bring your own cluster docs assume k3s. Installing on Talos on Hetzner (the banano cluster) needed several settings that are not written down anywhere. Each cost time to find.

**What to document (all seen on banano)**

* **Registry ClusterIP**: `registryClusterIP` defaults to 10.43.255.250, which only exists in k3s's service range. Talos with a 10.0.96.0/19 service CIDR needed 10.0.96.250, and the registry mirror set through Talos `machine.registries.mirrors` instead of k3s `registries.yaml` (containerd `hosts.toml` elsewhere).
* **User namespaces**: rootless buildkit needs `user.max_user_namespaces` set; hardened distros disable it.
* **Gateway API CRDs**: the cluster must not pre-install them. Envoy Gateway ships the experimental channel plus a safe-upgrades ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, and the hcloud-k8s Talos module installs the standard channel by default (`gateway_api_crds_enabled = false`).
* **Hetzner load balancer limits**: no UDP, lb11 allows 5 services. Unbind TCP/UDP routes land on the merged Envoy service.
* **Hetzner API budget**: 3600 requests an hour per project, shared by every token, a new token does not help. The Talos VIP drains it ([UNB-387](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-387/docs-talos-hcloud-vip-drains-the-hetzner-api-budget-csi-and-ccm-stop)).
* **hcloud CSI**: set `HCLOUD_VOLUME_DEFAULT_LOCATION` (`controller.hcloudVolumeDefaultLocation`), otherwise the controller needs the API to start and crashloops while the budget is empty, and no volume can attach anywhere.
* **API firewall**: the hcloud-k8s module opens 6443 and 50000 only to the IP it sees at plan time unless `firewall_api_source` is set. A VPN looks like a dead cluster.
* **Worker nodes and the LB**: with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, nodes without Envoy fail LB health checks; label them `node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers=true`.

**After the change**

A Talos/Hetzner install works the first time from the docs. The banano setup notes (`new-unbind/setup-notes.md`, `unbind-gaps.md`) are the source.

Related: [UNB-387](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-387/docs-talos-hcloud-vip-drains-the-hetzner-api-budget-csi-and-ccm-stop), [UNB-341](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-341/improve-docs).

issues.title: Variables mounted as files cannot hold references
issues.description:
A variable mounted as a file is written as a literal. `${{...}}` references in it are not rendered, so a config file that needs a database password or another service's address has to be pasted with the real values, and repeated on every service that uses it.

**Seen on banano**

* graham: the 4 server services repeat their bot's `CONFIG_YAML` as literals instead of referencing it.
* reddit: `tipper.ini` holds the database password, so it is rendered by a script (`new-unbind/reddit-secrets.py`) and has to be regenerated whenever the password changes.
* pippin (banano, nano, wban): each `CONFIG_YAML` mount holds the node RPC, websocket and work peer addresses as literals, so moving the nodes ([UNB-376](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-376/banano-move-banano-node-and-nano-node-into-the-new-project-network)) means editing three files by hand.

**After the change**

References in mounted files render like env variables and follow their source. A password rotation or node move updates the files and rolls out the services, no scripts.

**Proposal**

Render references in variable mounts with the same renderer as env variables, and include mounted variables in reference propagation.

issues.title: create-service refuses watch_paths
issues.description:
`create-service` has no `watch_paths` field (422 when sent over the API, absent from the MCP tool), while `update-service` accepts it. A monorepo service needs a create and then an update before its first push, or it deploys on every push to the repo in between.

**Seen on banano**

Every service that shares a repo was created, then updated with its watch paths: dux docs and api (DankLinux-Docs, `**,!server/**` and `server/**,blog/**`), [appditto.com](<http://appditto.com>) frontend and inquire, natrium-io site and help, MonKey server and frontend, natricon server, thebrownsboard nodebb.

**After the change**

Watch paths can be set in the create call, from the API, MCP and the create flow in the UI.

**Proposal**

Add `watch_paths` to the create input and pass it through like on update.

issues.title: Import existing data: volumes from a URL or S3, database restore from a backup
issues.description:
There is no way to bring existing data into Unbind. Volumes cannot be filled from an archive, existing PVCs cannot be adopted, and the database restore parameters in the definitions are not wired up.

**Seen on banano (whole migration, 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-14)**

* Every Postgres database (12 in the wallet wave alone, about 6 GB) moved with `pg_dump` streamed pod to pod and `pg_restore` by hand, with checksums and row counts compared by scripts (`new-unbind/wallet-cutover.sh`).
* Redis (five wban databases, about 360k keys) moved with a Lua DUMP/RESTORE script and a per-key digest compare (`new-unbind/wban-cutover.sh`).
* Volumes (synapse media 13 GB, the Ghost content dirs, beatrice sqlite) pulled as a tar to a local file and streamed into a helper pod, then compared with an `md5sum` of every file. Piping one `kubectl exec` straight into another cut off silently.
* The two Ghost blogs: deploy the template on a staging host, park it, drop its tables, import the MySQL dump, copy the content dir, unpark.

**After the change**

A volume or database can start from an archive (S3, URL or upload), and a database can restore from one of its own backups or another S3 dump. Moving onto Unbind, or recovering from a lost volume, does not need kubectl and custom scripts.

**Proposal**

* Volume import: an init job that downloads and unpacks a tar from S3 or a URL into a new volume.
* Database restore: wire up the existing restore parameters (WAL-G / pg_restore for Postgres, the MySQL and Redis equivalents) and offer "restore from backup" in the UI.

issues.title: Switch an image service to a git source, and move a domain between services in one step
issues.description:
An image service cannot become a git service ([UNB-339](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-339/ability-to-change-the-source-repository-and-branch-of-a-repo-after-a) changes the repo or the image, not the type). Replacing one with the other means creating a new service and moving the domain: removing it from the old service and adding it to the new one serves 404 or 503 for a few seconds and issues a new certificate.

**Seen on banano**

* dux danklinux `api` was created as an image service with an `api-data` volume, then had to be deleted (with its volume) and created again as a git service.
* Moving domains between services gave 8 to 13 s of 404, 503 or 525 per domain ([UNB-389](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-389/domain-changes-restart-the-service-with-downtime-for-services-with-a), [UNB-390](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-390/removing-a-domain-briefly-breaks-the-services-other-domains) cover the restart side). `apply-staged-changes` with both services in one call releases first and is the least bad option today.

**After the change**

A service keeps its id, variables, domains and volume while its source changes from image to git (or back). Moving a domain to another service is one operation without a gap.

**Proposal**

* Allow `type` to change on update between `docker-image` and `github`, rebuilding from the new source.
* A "move domain" operation that reassigns the host and keeps the certificate.

Related: [UNB-396](https://linear.app/unbind/issue/UNB-396/no-way-to-move-a-service-to-another-project-or-environment) (move a service to another project).

issues.title: List GitHub installations over the API and MCP
issues.description:
`create-service` needs a `github_installation_id`, but installations are not exposed over the API or MCP. An agent cannot find out which installation to use.

**Seen on banano**

Every git service created over MCP during the migration needed the installation id, read straight from the database (`github_installations` joined to `github_apps` and `teams` in pg-unbind). The wban team's new installation on appditto for pippin (171224543) and the yekta team's on yekta (171231275) were found the same way.

**After the change**

A read-only `list-github-installations` (team scoped: id, account, repository selection) lets the UI, API clients and agents pick the right installation without database access.

**Proposal**

A list endpoint and MCP tool returning the installations the caller's team can use. Possibly a repository search per installation, since `create-service` fails when the repo is not covered.

issues.title: Share one GitHub connection with several teams
issues.description:
A GitHub App connection belongs to one team, so every team that builds from the same GitHub account needs its own app installed on that account.

**Seen on banano**

* appditto/pippin_nano_wallet is built by the banano team and by the wban team, so the appditto account has installations from the appditto, banano and wban teams.
* yekta's account has installations from the banano team (chat-banano-cc) and the yekta team (dashboard). The yekta team could not deploy its dashboard until yekta installed a second app.
* BananoCoin has installations from the banano and wban teams.

**After the change**

One installation per GitHub account, shared with the teams that should build from it, chosen in the UI. New teams can build without another approval from the account owner.

**Proposal**

Let a system admin (or the connection's owner) grant a connection to several teams, with repo access still limited by the installation.

issues.title: Pass the git commit to builds and running services
issues.description:
Builds do not get the commit SHA or branch as a build argument or environment variable, so apps that stamp their version from CI lose it.

**Seen on banano**

dlx-docs-server stamped its version from CI and under Unbind reports `development`. Any app that shows its version in a health or about endpoint has the same problem.

**After the change**

`UNBIND_GIT_SHA` and `UNBIND_GIT_BRANCH` are available as Docker build args (railpack too) and as runtime env, so versions and error reports name the deployed commit.

**Proposal**

Pass both as build args when the Dockerfile declares them, and set them as env on the deployment. Document them with the other Unbind provided variables.

issues.title: Check for updates button
issues.description:
The update list is cached for 10 minutes in Redis on top of about 5 minutes of GitHub raw CDN caching, so a new release can take up to 15 minutes to show up in Settings.

**Seen on banano**

To apply releases right after tagging, `unbind-updater:updates` was deleted from the platform Redis by hand nine times between 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-14.

**After the change**

A "Check for updates" button on the updates page refetches the release metadata and clears the cache, so a release shows up as soon as its metadata is on GitHub.

**Proposal**

Button (system admin only) that deletes the cache key and refetches, bypassing the CDN with a cache-busting query or the GitHub API.

issues.title: [F48] Template inputs endpoint returns raw secret values to Viewers and to API keys without read_variable_values
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence high), CWE-863
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/service_group/template_inputs.go:205` in `resolveInputs`

## Impact

Secret values of template-deployed services are disclosed to principals the platform deliberately blocks from seeing variable values. These include database and admin credentials, signing keys and API keys that unlock write access to those systems.

## What

GetTemplateInputs only requires ActionViewer on the environment (line 46), then reads every group service's Kubernetes secret and copies the plaintext into CurrentValue for variable inputs (205) and generated display variables (294). Nothing checks Editor or the read_variable_values privilege, and nothing calls Redact. GetVariables enforces both, and AGENTS.md says values must come back redacted without the privilege.

## Exploit scenario

A user who only has Viewer on an environment, or a read-only MCP connected app or API key without read_variable_values, calls GET /service_groups/template-inputs (MCP tool get-service-group-template-inputs) for any template-deployed group. The response holds the plaintext template variables, such as admin passwords and SMTP/API tokens, plus generated admin keys exposed as display variables.

## Preconditions

* Authenticated principal with Viewer on the environment (session, API key or connected app)
* The environment contains a service group deployed from a template

## Fix

Redact CurrentValue for variable and display inputs unless the caller passes the same check as VariablesService.canReadValues: Editor for sessions, and read_variable_values plus owner Editor for keys and apps. Alternatively gate the operation with oapi.Needs(read_variable_values) and require Editor.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F48, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F49] Service group info endpoint returns plaintext secret variables to Viewers
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence high), CWE-863
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/service_group/info.go:160` in `variableInfos`

## Impact

Credentials and signing keys stored as service variables are disclosed to read-only principals. This bypasses the platform's value-visibility policy.

## What

GetServiceGroupInfo checks only ActionViewer on the environment (lines 19-28). variableInfos then reads each service's secret and returns the raw value of every variable that has metadata (template inputs, derived keys, display variables), with no privilege check or redaction.

## Exploit scenario

A team member with only Viewer on an environment, or an API key with read-only role and no privileges, calls GET /service_groups/info for a template-deployed group. They receive plaintext values such as generated JWT secrets, ANON/SERVICE_ROLE keys and admin passwords that GetVariables would redact for them.

## Preconditions

* Authenticated principal with Viewer on the environment
* A template-deployed service group with variable metadata exists

## Fix

Apply the same value-visibility decision as GetVariables (Editor for sessions, read_variable_values for keys and apps) and blank Value otherwise.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F49, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F50] Redis is used without authentication although its queue holds GitHub App private keys, registry passwords and service secrets
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence high), CWE-306
**Where:** `apps/api/cmd/api/main.go:94` in `startAPI`

## Impact

Cross-tenant credential theft: GitHub App private keys, container registry credentials, and other teams' service variables and database URLs. Integrity loss is also likely: forged builder jobs and supply-chain image tampering, plus redirect_uri tampering for cached OAuth clients.

## What

The API builds its only Redis client with a hard-coded empty password, so Redis auth cannot be turned on. The shipped helmfile deploys Redis with auth.enabled=false and protected-mode off, and the repo defines no NetworkPolicy. The deployment queue in that Redis stores full build environments, including GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, CONTAINER_REGISTRY_PASSWORD, SERVICE_BUILD_SECRETS and ADDITIONAL_ENV, as plaintext JSON. Any pod that can reach redis-headless.unbind-system:6379 can read these secrets and change the queue.

## Exploit scenario

A user with deploy rights in team A, or an attacker who has exploited a public app running on Unbind, starts a pod that connects to redis-headless.unbind-system:6379 and runs MONITOR, or polls ZRANGE on the builder queue key. Every deployment any team enqueues is then visible as a ZADD carrying the base64 build secrets, the GitHub App private key and the internal registry username and password. With the GitHub App key the attacker can mint installation tokens for every repo the app can reach, across all teams. With the registry credentials they can push backdoored images under other teams' repositories. The attacker can also ZADD forged queue items (env such as DEPLOYMENT_NAMESPACE or SERVICE_IMAGE) that processJob hands to k8s.CreateDeployment. They can also poison the unbind:cimd OAuth client-metadata cache that oauthserver/cimd.go trusts.

## Preconditions

* Attacker can run code in any pod on the cluster network. Examples: a team member who can deploy any service, or an attacker who has compromised a deployed tenant app.
* Default chart deployment (Redis auth disabled, no NetworkPolicies)

## Fix

Make the Redis password configurable (REDIS_PASSWORD or a redis:// URL parsed with redis.ParseURL) and enable auth in the helmfile Redis release with a generated secret. Add NetworkPolicies so only unbind-system workloads can reach Redis, Postgres and Loki. Stop putting raw secrets in queue payloads: enqueue only the deployment ID and resolve secrets when the builder Job is created.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F50, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F51] Build job queue runs on unauthenticated Redis that tenant workloads can reach, so any team can inject or read build jobs
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence high), CWE-306
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/queue/redis_queue.go:141` in `(*Queue[T]).DequeueN`

## Impact

Cross-tenant theft of service secrets and build secrets. Arbitrary workloads deployed into any namespace with any secret mounted, including the platform's own namespace, which leads to takeover of the Unbind instance and its database credentials. Other teams' services and domains can be hijacked.

## What

DequeueN reads members of the Redis sorted set 'unbind:build:queue' and hands them to deployctl.processJob as trusted DeploymentJobRequests. Redis has no authentication (Password "" in cmd/api/main.go, auth.enabled false and protected-mode no in the helmfile), and no NetworkPolicy exists anywhere in the repo, so any pod a tenant runs can write to the queue. processJob passes req.Environment unchanged into the builder Job, which runs as a ServiceAccount with cluster-wide rights on unbind Service CRDs.

## Exploit scenario

An editor in any team deploys a Docker image service and opens a shell in it, then connects to redis-headless.unbind-system:6379, which needs no password. (1) Read: they poll ZRANGE unbind:build:queue 0 -1 and collect every queued job's SERVICE_BUILD_SECRETS and ADDITIONAL_ENV, i.e. the variables and secrets of other teams' services. (2) Write: they ZADD a crafted item whose id is one of their own deployment IDs and whose environment holds DEPLOYMENT_NAMESPACE=<victim namespace or unbind-system>, SERVICE_NAME=<target CRD>, SERVICE_IMAGE=<attacker image>, SERVICE_SECRET_NAME=<target secret>. The API's processor creates a builder Job with that environment. The builder skips the build because an image is given, and creates or updates the unbind Service CRD in the target namespace using its cluster-wide ServiceAccount. The operator then runs the attacker's image with the target's secrets. The same Redis also holds the unbind:cimd:\* OAuth client-metadata cache, which oauthserver.MetadataFetcher.Fetch trusts without re-validating. Poisoning a client's redirect_uris lets the attacker steal authorization codes once a victim consents.

## Preconditions

* Attacker is an authenticated user who can run a workload, e.g. editor in any team creating a Docker image service
* Default install: Redis chart with auth disabled and no NetworkPolicy isolating unbind-system from team namespaces

## Fix

Enable Redis authentication (requirepass/ACL), pass the password from a secret instead of hard-coding Password "", and turn protected-mode back on. Add NetworkPolicies so only the API can reach Redis; the same exposure applies to Loki (auth_enabled: false), Prometheus and the registry. Do not trust queue items as is: carry only the deployment ID and rebuild the builder environment from the database when the job is processed, or HMAC-sign queue items and cache entries and verify them on read. Keep secrets out of Redis.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F51, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F52] Domain redirect URL lets a user inject nginx directives into the shared ingress-nginx configuration-snippet
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence high), CWE-74
**Where:** `apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/nginx.go:69` in `nginxSnippet`

## Impact

Arbitrary directive injection into the cluster-wide ingress-nginx configuration. Likely outcomes are reading files from the controller pod (its service account token can read secrets cluster-wide) and cross-tenant traffic manipulation or denial of service. The exact impact depends on ingress-nginx runtime protections such as annotation-value-word-blocklist. I could not verify those protections without running the controller.

## What

A team editor sets [HostSpec.Redirect.To](<http://HostSpec.Redirect.To>) through create, update or apply-staged-changes on a service. The API's validateRedirect (apps/api/internal/services/service/host_options.go:104) checks only the scheme, the hostname, and that there is no query, fragment or userinfo. It never checks the path. The proxy path gets proxyPathPattern but the redirect path does not. The operator's parseURLTarget (hostoptions.go:126) copies the percent-decoded url.Path, so %3B, %0A, %20 and %22 become a literal ';', a newline, a space and a quote. nginxSnippet then writes that path verbatim into the [nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet](<http://nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet>) annotation.

## Exploit scenario

An editor in team A updates a service domain with [redirect.to](<http://redirect.to>) = "[https://example.com/x%3B%0A%7D%0Alocation%20/leak%20%7B%20alias%20/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/%3B%20%7D%0Alocation%20/y%20%7B%23](<https://example.com/x%3B%0A%7D%0Alocation%20/leak%20%7B%20alias%20/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/%3B%20%7D%0Alocation%20/y%20%7B%23>)". There is no '?' and no literal '#', so it passes validateRedirect. The operator renders "return 308 [https://example.com/x;\\n](<https://example.com/x;%5Cn>)}\\nlocation /leak { alias /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/; }..." into the configuration-snippet, and ingress-nginx inserts it into the shared nginx.conf. The attacker then requests https://<their-host>/leak/token to read the controller's service account token, which can read secrets in every namespace. That exposes other teams' database passwords and Unbind's own credentials. Even a payload that only breaks the config syntax stops ingress reloads for every tenant, because admission webhooks are disabled.

## Preconditions

* The installation uses the nginx networking provider (networkingProvider=nginx; the chart default is gateway)
* The attacker is an authenticated user, API key or OAuth grant with editor rights on a service in any team

## Fix

Apply a strict path check to redirect URLs in validateRedirect, as is already done for proxies, for example pathSegmentPattern or proxyPathPattern on the decoded target.Path. In the operator, build snippet values from the escaped form (url.URL.EscapedPath) and reject any ';', whitespace, quote, brace, '$' or control character before writing to configuration-snippet. Better still, use native ingress-nginx annotations (permanent-redirect) instead of raw snippets.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F52, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F53] In-cluster image registry has no authentication, so any tenant pod can pull or overwrite every team's images
issues.description:
**Severity:** HIGH (confidence medium), CWE-306
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/infrastructure/registrycache/registry_config.go:22` in `registryConfig (applied by Manager.MigrateRegistryConfig)`

## Impact

Cross-tenant confidentiality loss of private images, and cross-tenant code execution with the victim service's secrets through tag overwrite.

## What

The distribution config the API writes into the docker-registry ConfigMap, matching the chart, has no auth section. The registry is a plain ClusterIP service at docker-registry.<system-ns>:5000 with no NetworkPolicy, and it is the default build registry. Any pod in any team namespace can therefore list, pull, push and delete every repository without credentials. The operator deploys services with ImagePullPolicy Always, so an overwritten tag is pulled on the victim's next pod start.

## Exploit scenario

From a pod in their own team namespace, an attacker calls GET [http://docker-registry.unbind-system:5000/v2/\_catalog](<http://docker-registry.unbind-system:5000/v2/_catalog>) and /v2/<repo>/tags/list to enumerate every team's built images. They pull any of them, which exposes compiled source and anything baked in at build time. They then push a malicious image over the tag a victim service runs. On the victim's next rollout, restart, scale or reschedule, kubelet pulls the attacker's image (PullAlways), and it runs in the victim's namespace with the victim's environment variables and secrets.

## Preconditions

* Attacker can run a workload in some team namespace, e.g. as a team editor
* Default install with the bundled registry and no NetworkPolicy

## Fix

Configure registry auth (htpasswd or token) in registryConfig and the chart, and give the builder push credentials and kubelet pull credentials only. Restrict network access to the registry with a NetworkPolicy. Consider per-team repositories with scoped tokens, or deploying by digest so tag overwrites have no effect.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F53, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F54] System editor can add themselves to the superuser group and become system admin
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-269
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/group/user_mutations.go:39` in `AddUserToGroup`

## Impact

Vertical privilege escalation from a delegated system-editor role to full instance admin: all teams, users, credentials and settings.

## What

Granting permissions to a group requires system admin (permissions.go GrantPermissionToGroup), but adding a member to any non-team group needs only system editor. Nothing compares the target group's grants with the requester's own, so a system editor can join the 'superuser' group (system admin and team admin superuser) and inherit admin.

## Exploit scenario

An admin delegates system editor to an operator group. A member calls POST /groups/members/add with group_id=<superuser group> and user_id=<self>. Check passes on system editor, and the user now holds system admin and admin on every team. RemoveUserFromGroup also lets them remove real admins from the group.

## Preconditions

* Attacker has been granted editor on the system resource (a non-default, admin-delegated role)

## Fix

Require system admin to add or remove members of groups that carry system or superuser grants, or refuse to add a user to a group whose grants exceed the requester's own.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F54, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F55] Public password login has no rate limiting or lockout
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-307
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/api/handlers/auth/login.go:35` in `Login`

## Impact

Online password guessing against every account, including system admins. A hit gives full account takeover.

## What

POST /auth/login is registered public, with no middleware (router.go:170 register("/auth", ..., false, ...)), and it checks attacker-supplied email/password pairs with no attempt counter, delay or lockout. The app has a Redis RateLimiter, but it is only mounted on the /oauth/\* and /mcp routes (main.go:339, oauthserver/handler.go:47-49).

## Exploit scenario

An internet attacker who knows or guesses an admin email (for example from the timing oracle in Authenticate) sends many parallel login requests with candidate passwords. Nothing in the API slows or blocks them. A successful guess returns full session cookies.

## Preconditions

* The API is reachable over the network
* The target account's password can be guessed (minimum length is 8)

## Fix

Rate limit /auth/login per client IP and per account with the existing RateLimiter, add progressive delays or temporary lockout, and alert on repeated failures.

---

Source: security scan of fb0061a2 on 2026-10-15, finding F55, confirmed 3/3 by the review panel. Found by reading code, not by running an exploit.

issues.title: [F56] UpdateWebhook lets a caller rewrite another team's or project's webhook URL by passing an unrelated team_id or project_id
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-639
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/webooks/update.go:58` in `UpdateWebhook`

## Impact

An attacker can tamper with webhooks across tenants and above their own scope: they can redirect deployment and project notifications, which carry team, project, environment, service and deployment IDs plus names, to a URL they control, and silence the victim's alerts.

## What

The body's team_id and project_id are attacker-controlled. They feed a Permissions().Check that passes if any one entry passes (checker.go:74), and nothing ties the two IDs to each other. The ownership test afterwards compares only team_id for team webhooks and only project_id for project webhooks, so the caller can satisfy the check with a resource they own and use the other ID to reach the victim's webhook.

## Exploit scenario

Team webhook: an editor of team A (which implies editor on A's projects) or a user who only has project-scoped editor on P_a sends PUT /webhooks/update with {id: <victim team webhook>, team_id: <victim team>, project_id: P_a, url: [https://attacker/x](<https://attacker/x>)}. The check passes on P_a, line 45 passes because team_id matches the webhook, and the URL is replaced. Every later team event (project created/updated/deleted) for the victim team then goes to the attacker. Project webhook: a team-A editor sends {id: <victim project webhook>, team_id: A, project_id: <victim project>}. The check passes on team A, line 49 passes, and the webhook is rewritten. The same path lets an API key scoped to one project modify team-level webhooks of its owner's team.

## Preconditions

* Attacker is an editor on some team, or holds project-scoped editor (custom group or scoped API key)

issues.title: [F58] Nested variable reference expansion is exponential, so stored references can pin API CPU
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-407, CWE-770
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/variables/render.go:280` in `renderNested`

## Impact

Availability of the shared API process. Each GetVariables call on the affected service (viewer access is enough), each UpdateVariables response, and each deployment render (deployctl.go:479, 817; deployments/redeploy.go:24) burns a CPU core for an effectively unbounded time, across all teams on the install.

## What

Stored ${{...}} references are rendered recursively up to maxReferenceDepth (8) with no memoization, and vartemplate.Render calls the resolver once per occurrence, not once per distinct token. A value with k copies of a reference to another value that itself has k copies costs about k^9 resolutions. Team, project and environment writes skip validateReferences entirely, and service writes only reject a variable that references itself by the same key, so two variables that reference each other many times are accepted. Also CWE-770: Stored variable values, which an Editor on any single service controls, are resolved recursively by resolveAt and renderNested. Only the chain depth is limited (maxReferenceDepth = 8). Fan-out per level, total output size and total work are not. vartemplate.Render calls the resolver once for every occurrence of a token, not once per distinct token, and nothing caches the rendered results. Each nested level therefore multiplies the output by the number of repeated tokens, and the rendered string is built in memory.

## Exploit scenario

An editor stores two service variables that each reference the other dozens of times, or a team variable that references itself dozens of times plus a service variable that references it. The write response and every later view or deployment of that service starts a render that does not finish. Repeated calls use up API CPU.

## Preconditions

* Editor on a service (service variables), or Editor on a team, project or environment (scope variables) to store the values

## Fix

Memoize resolved values per (source, key) inside renderContext, cap total resolutions or output size per render, check ctx cancellation in the resolver, and reject reference cycles and oversized token counts at write time for every scope type. Also CWE-770: Cap expansion, not just depth. Memoize the rendered value per (source, key) inside renderContext, and limit the total rendered length, for example to the 1 MiB Kubernetes secret limit, plus the number of resolver calls per render. Return an unresolved or error result once a limit is hit. Also reject reference cycles between a service's own keys at write time, and apply validateReferences to team/project/environment scope writes.

issues.title: [F62] Webhook response body from an attacker-chosen URL is read into memory with no size limit or timeout
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-770
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/webooks/trigger.go:157` in `sendDefaultWebhook`

## Impact

Memory exhaustion and a crash of the multi-tenant API server, a denial of service for all teams. The attacker can trigger it again whenever they like.

## What

A team or project editor sets the webhook URL to any host (models/webhook_input.go:12 only enforces format:uri). When the response is not 200, sendDefaultWebhook reads the whole body with io.ReadAll and no cap, using an http.Client{} that has no Timeout (webhooks.go:20). It then copies the body into the error string, which errors.Join keeps and both trigger.go:96 and the caller log again.

## Exploit scenario

An attacker with editor rights on a project creates a project webhook pointing at a server they control, then creates or updates a service, which fires TriggerWebhooks in a background goroutine inside the API process. Their server answers HTTP 500 and streams a body of several gigabytes, or one that never ends. The API buffers all of it and then copies it several more times into error strings and log lines. Registering several such webhooks, or firing several events at once, multiplies the memory used until the shared API pod is OOM-killed. That takes the API down for every team on the instance, and the attacker can repeat it on each later event.

## Preconditions

* Attacker is authenticated with editor on a team or project, so they can create a webhook
* Attacker controls an HTTP server reachable from the API pod
* A webhook event (project/service create, update or delete, deployment, cron failure) fires

## Fix

Wrap resp.Body in io.LimitReader (for example 4 KiB) before reading it for the error message, set a Timeout on the webhook http.Client and limit redirects. Do not put raw response bodies or the full webhook URL into errors or logs.

issues.title: [F63] Secret webhook URLs (Slack/Discord tokens, Telegram bot token) are written to build logs that service viewers and read_logs API keys can query
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence high), CWE-532
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/webooks/trigger.go:96` in `TriggerWebhooks`

## Impact

Webhook credentials leak across both the role boundary (viewer vs editor) and the key privilege boundary (read_logs vs read_webhook_urls). Holders can post forged messages into team chat channels (phishing teammates with fake deploy alerts) or fully control a Telegram bot.

A project has a deployment webhook. Either it points at a generic endpoint that answers 202 or 204 (treated as a failure, so the URL is logged on every deploy), or it is a Telegram/Slack URL that sometimes returns 4xx/429. A team viewer, who cannot list project webhooks because that needs project editor, opens Build logs for any deployment of a service in the project, or calls query-logs with type=build. Sanitize errors from [httpClient.Do](<http://httpClient.Do>) (unwrap \*url.Error and drop .URL) before logging or returning them, and keep webhook delivery errors out of the builder's user-visible output. issues.title: [F66] UpdateService trusts team/project/environment IDs from the body without binding them to the service, which weakens the cross-team domain conflict check
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-639, CWE-863
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/service/update.go:397` in `applyServiceUpdate`

## Impact

Cross-tenant hijacking of path prefixes on another team's domain (traffic and credential interception), mounting of unattached volumes from environments the caller cannot access, and spoofed notifications to another team's webhooks.

## What

prepareServiceUpdate checks Editor on input.ServiceID and that the body's team/project/environment are consistent with each other (VerifyInputs). It never checks that the loaded service lives in them, unlike RestartServiceByID, GetDNSForService and scheduledService. input.TeamID then becomes the 'same team' scope in CountHostConflicts, where same-team services only conflict on an identical host+path and wildcards are not checked for overlap. Also CWE-863: UpdateService authorizes only editor on input.ServiceID. VerifyInputs then checks that the supplied environment/project/team chain is internally consistent, but not that the service belongs to it. CountHostConflicts (repositories/service/queries.go:247) treats the teamID argument as the claimant's team: same-team services may share a host on different paths, while other teams' hosts are exclusive. A caller who passes another team's IDs is treated as that team.

## Exploit scenario

An Editor of a service in team A who knows team B's team/project/environment IDs (for example as a Viewer member of B or a former member) sends update-service for their own service with B's IDs and upsert_hosts \[{host: [app.victim.com](<http://app.victim.com>), path: /api}\]. B's services are treated as the same team, so the claim passes as long as B does not already hold that exact path. On a controller that merges routes for one hostname across namespaces (ingress-nginx does this), requests to [app.victim.com/api](<http://app.victim.com/api>) would reach the attacker's service, along with the victim domain's cookies. This depends on how the routing controller behaves, which was not verified by running it. With the same trick inside one team, a PVC scoped to another project/environment can be mounted, and update webhooks fire to the chosen team.

## Preconditions

* Editor on any service
* Knowledge of a victim team's team, project and environment UUIDs
* For traffic interception, a routing controller that merges same-host routes across namespaces

## Fix

After loading the service, require service.EnvironmentID == input.EnvironmentID (and therefore the project and team), or derive team/project/environment from the service and ignore the body values. Do the same in ApplyStagedChanges. Also CWE-863: Derive the team from the service itself (service.Edges.Environment.Edges.Project.TeamID) and reject the request when input.EnvironmentID/ProjectID/TeamID do not match the stored service. Better, have CountHostConflicts look up the team from excludingServiceID instead of taking it as a parameter.

issues.title: [F67] An inviter can redeem their own invitation link to pre-register an account for someone else's email

issues.title: [F68] Form-urlencoded body decoder allows nested sparse-slice amplification (multi-GB allocation per request)
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-770
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/api/router/router.go:76` in `urlEncodedFormat.Unmarshal`

## Impact

Denial of service of the Unbind API server (control plane) through memory exhaustion or OOM kill. Any authenticated user can trigger it.

## What

Any huma operation accepts an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body, because the format is registered globally (router.go:126-127). The attacker's dotted keys go to a default gorilla/schema decoder (router.go:47). It caps each slice index at 16000, but the cap applies separately at every nesting level. A body struct with a slice of structs that holds another slice of structs therefore allocates about 16000 x 16000 elements from a body under 1 MiB.

## Exploit scenario

An authenticated user (any session, or a write-capable API key) sends POST /staged-changes/apply with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The body holds 16001 pairs of the form Variables.<i>.Upserts.16000.Name=a for i=0..16000, about 590 KB, which fits huma's 1 MiB limit. huma's schema validation rejects the dotted keys with 422, but parseBodyInto still calls urlEncodedFormat.Unmarshal. gorilla/schema then builds a 16001-element outer slice and, under each element, a 16001-element \[\]VariableUpsertInput, about 8 GB of heap. A few repeated or concurrent requests should push the API process past its memory limit, or into GC thrashing, and take down the control-plane API for every tenant.

## Preconditions

* Attacker holds any valid session, or an API key that allows writes (read-only keys are refused by allowNarrowed before the body is parsed)
* The target operation's body is a non-pointer struct with a nested slice of structs (e.g. apply-staged-changes)

## Fix

Remove the global x-www-form-urlencoded format unless a real client needs it, or limit it to the operations that do. If it stays: call decoder.MaxSize with a small value, call decoder.IgnoreUnknownKeys(false), and skip decoding when validation failed. Also consider rejecting dotted or indexed keys before Decode.

issues.title: [F72] Redirect target path is not limited to a safe character set before reaching ingress config
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-20
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/service/host_options.go:106` in `validateRedirect`

## Impact

On installs using the nginx networking provider, a service editor can put unvalidated text into the shared ingress controller's configuration. That reaches beyond the tenant, and even a malformed value can break config reloads for every service.

## What

The comment on validateHostOptions says these values land in proxy config verbatim, so the character set has to stay narrow. validateProxy enforces that with proxyPathPattern, but validateRedirect checks only scheme, host, query, fragment and userinfo, never the decoded path. The operator's nginx provider (apps/operator/internal/resourcebuilder/networking/nginx.go:69) writes that decoded path into an ingress-nginx configuration-snippet, and the bundled chart enables snippet annotations.

## Exploit scenario

Not worked out here. The concern is that the redirect path is the one host option without the character restriction the code's own comment requires, and it ends up in a config snippet.

## Preconditions

* networkingProvider set to nginx (the documented migration path for existing clusters; not the default for new installs)
* Editor on a service or environment able to set host redirects

## Fix

Apply the same narrow path validation to redirect targets as to proxy targets (check the decoded path against proxyPathPattern or stricter, and reject control characters, whitespace, quotes, semicolons and braces). Also escape or quote values in the operator's nginx snippet builder.

issues.title: [F73] Unvalidated ${{service:<id>.KEY}} tokens in environment variables or template inputs let an environment editor read any service secret in the project
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-639
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/variables/render.go:265` in `resolveAt`

## Impact

A principal confined to one environment can read the secrets and connection strings of any service in other environments of the same project, which breaks environment- and resource-scoped RBAC and API-key scoping.

## What

The render path resolves any service UUID named in a token, including nested tokens inside team/project/environment values, as long as the source is in the same project. It never checks the requester's access to that source. The only access check, validateReferences, runs only for service-scope writes (write.go:115), so tokens in environment-scope variables and in template input values reach the renderer unchecked.

## Exploit scenario

A user or scoped API key/connected app holds Editor only on the 'staging' environment of a project. It writes environment variable X=${{service:<prod-db-id>.DATABASE_PASSWORD}}. The write is only checked for Editor on staging, so it passes. Next it sets Y=${{environment.X}} on a staging service it controls; validateReferences only needs Viewer on staging, so that passes too. Reading that service's variables, or the pod environment after deploy, returns the production database password through renderNested. DeployTemplate and UpdateTemplateInputs input values can carry the same token directly.

## Preconditions

* Editor on some environment of the project (session, API key or connected app)
* Knowledge of the target service's UUID (it can show up in references, webhook links or shared URLs)

## Fix

Run the reference checks (same project, and an access check strong enough to read values) on every write that can store tokens: team/project/environment variables, template deploy inputs and template input edits. Also bind resolution to the writer's authority: reject or leave unresolved any nested service token whose source the scope's writers could not reference.

issues.title: [F74] Deleting a service group with delete_services needs only environment Editor, while deleting a service needs Admin
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-863
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/service_group/delete.go:20` in `DeleteServiceGroup`

## Impact

Editors can destroy services and their stored variables, which the platform reserves for Admins. The result is loss of availability and of secret data.

## What

DeleteServiceByID requires ActionAdmin on the service, and environments and projects also need Admin to delete. DeleteServiceGroup with DeleteServices=true deletes every member service's CR, secret and DB row after checking only Editor on the environment. UpdateServiceGroup, also Editor, can first add any ungrouped service in the environment to the group.

## Exploit scenario

An environment Editor, or an Editor-role API key, cannot delete the production database service directly because that needs Admin. They create a service group, add the database service to it with update-service-group, then call delete-service-group with delete_services=true. The service, its workload and its secret are removed.

## Preconditions

* Editor on the environment

## Fix

When DeleteServices is set, require Admin on the environment or on each member service, matching DeleteServiceByID.

issues.title: [F75] Template input values bypass reference validation, letting ${{...}} tokens read secrets the deployer cannot access
issues.description:
**Severity:** MEDIUM (confidence medium), CWE-863
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/templates/deploy.go:406` in `DeployTemplate`

## Impact

Secrets of other environments and of team/project scopes in the same project leak to a user with editor on any environment of that project. This crosses the per-environment grant boundary.

## What

User-supplied template input values become variable values unchanged: GeneratorTypeInput returns AddPrefix+input. They are then written to the new service's secret without validateReferences, the only check on ${{service:<id>.KEY}} and ${{team|project|environment.KEY}} tokens. UpdateTemplateInputs (template_inputs.go:476-480, :526) does the same. At deploy and read time the renderer resolves a token against any service in the same project (inProject) or the team/project secret. It never checks whether the requester can access the source.

## Exploit scenario

A user who is editor only on the staging environment deploys the Gluetun template with input_vpn_provider set to ${{service:<prod-postgres-id>.DATABASE_PASSWORD}} or ${{team.STRIPE_KEY}}. Writing that value through the variables API would fail the permission checks in validateReferences. Here it is stored as is. The deployment renders the production secret into the new pod's env, and GetVariables on the new service (the attacker is editor there) returns it as resolved_value.

## Preconditions

* Attacker has editor on some environment of the project (fine-grained grant, not team-wide)
* Attacker knows the source service UUID or the team/project key name
* A template with a variable-type input is available (e.g. Gluetun)

## Fix

Run variable values produced from template inputs (DeployTemplate and UpdateTemplateInputs) through VariablesService.validateReferences, or reject ${{...}} tokens in input values. Consider also checking source access at render time for API responses.

issues.title: [F76] Login timing reveals which emails have accounts (bcrypt only runs for existing users)
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence high), CWE-208
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/repositories/user/queries.go:41` in `Authenticate`

## Impact

Remote, unauthenticated enumeration of registered user emails on the instance.

## What

The public, unauthenticated POST /auth/login (handlers/auth/login.go:35) calls Authenticate. For an unknown email it returns right after the DB lookup. For a known email it runs bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword at DefaultCost, which takes tens of milliseconds. The response time therefore shows whether the account exists, and the login route has no rate limiter.

## Exploit scenario

An unauthenticated attacker sends POST /auth/login with candidate emails and any password and measures latency. Responses that take about bcrypt time mark existing accounts. Those accounts are then targeted for password guessing or phishing.

## Preconditions

* Network access to the API

## Fix

When the user is not found, run bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword against a fixed dummy hash so both paths cost the same. Also rate-limit /auth/login.

---

issues.title: [F77] CreateRedeployment accepts a deployment ID from any service (IDOR)
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence high), CWE-639
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/deployments/redeploy.go:148` in `CreateRedeployment`

## Impact

Cross-tenant integrity damage to another service's deployment history, and the ability to run and inspect another team's private built image in the attacker's namespace.

## What

The permission check covers only input.ServiceID. The deployment is then loaded by its ID alone and never checked against deployment.ServiceID == input.ServiceID, a check that CancelDeployment performs (deployctl.go:676). The other service's deployment drives CreateCopy, which keeps the victim's ServiceID, and supplies the image and build settings.

## Exploit scenario

An Editor of a docker-image service in team A calls redeploy-deployment with their own service_id and the deployment_id of a service in team B, with smart_redeploy=true. The API creates a 'succeeded' manual deployment row under team B's service, which pollutes its history with team A's resource definition. It then runs team B's built image (often a private image in the internal registry) as team A's service, and returns the image reference. Without smart redeploy, B's build settings and commit SHA are fed into A's build.

## Preconditions

* Editor on any service
* Knowledge of a victim deployment UUID (random v4)

## Fix

Reject the request unless deployment.ServiceID == input.ServiceID, as CancelDeployment does, before any use of the deployment.

---

issues.title: [F78] Changing or resetting a password leaves existing session refresh tokens valid for up to 14 days
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence high), CWE-613
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/user/update.go:54` in `UpdatePassword`

## Impact

Changing the credential does not cut off a hijacked session.

## What

POST /users/update-password (handlers/user/update.go:34) only rewrites the bcrypt hash. Session refresh tokens in Oauth2Token are not revoked. They are not rotated either, and the auth middleware accepts them until they expire, minting new access tokens without checking when the password changed.

## Exploit scenario

An attacker who has stolen a user's refresh cookie keeps using it after the user changes their password, or after a system admin resets it in response to the compromise. The middleware keeps minting fresh access tokens from the old refresh token until its 14-day expiry.

## Preconditions

* Attacker already holds a victim's refresh token cookie

## Fix

Revoke all Oauth2Token rows for the user when the password changes (optionally keeping the caller's current session), and consider rotating refresh tokens on use.

---

issues.title: [F80] A system editor can redirect SMTP settings to their own host while keeping the stored password, exfiltrating the SMTP credential
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-522
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/email/email.go:79` in `UpdateSettings`

## Impact

Disclosure of the instance's SMTP relay credential, a write-only secret, which also opens the external mail account.

## What

A system editor can change host, port and encryption without re-supplying the password (a nil password means 'keep the stored one'). settings() then loads the stored secret from the unbind-smtp Kubernetes secret and sends it to the new host. With encryption=none the sender uses SMTPAuthPlainNoEnc, so the stored password goes to an editor-chosen server in cleartext.

## Exploit scenario

A system editor reads the current settings (the username is returned, the password is not), then PUTs the email settings with host=attacker.example, port=25, encryption=none, the same username and no password field. They then call the send-test endpoint. The API connects to the attacker's SMTP listener and authenticates with AUTH PLAIN using the stored relay password.

## Preconditions

* Attacker holds system editor
* An admin has configured SMTP with a username and password

## Fix

Clear or require re-entry of the stored password whenever host, port, username or encryption changes, or restrict SMTP setting changes to system admin.

---

issues.title: [F81] Stored SMTP password is sent to a new relay host when email settings change without re-entering it
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-522
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/email/email.go:72` in `UpdateSettings`

## Impact

A write-only credential for the organization's mail relay is disclosed to a less-privileged system editor.

## What

PUT /system/email/update (handlers/system/email.go:44) lets a system editor change host, port and encryption while omitting password, so the stored SMTP password is kept. SendTest (handlers/system/email.go:81) then authenticates to the new host with it. The API says the password is never returned, but an editor can recover it this way.

## Exploit scenario

A user with system editor but not admin rights sets host to an SMTP server they control, with encryption none, and leaves password out of the body. They then call send-test-email, and the server performs AUTH PLAIN against their host with the stored relay password.

## Preconditions

* Attacker holds system editor permission
* An SMTP password is already stored

## Fix

Clear or require the password again whenever host, port, username or encryption changes, and refuse to reuse the stored secret for a different relay.

---

issues.title: [F82] Login CSRF: /auth/login accepts cross-site form posts with no Origin or CSRF check
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-352
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/api/router/router.go:170` in `RegisterRoutes`

## Impact

Session fixation into an attacker-controlled account. Data the victim enters afterward goes to the attacker's teams.

## What

The /auth group is registered with authed=false, so the CSRF middleware (Origin allow-list plus double-submit token) is never attached to POST /auth/login. NewHumaConfig also registers an application/x-www-form-urlencoded format for every huma operation (router.go:126-127). Together these let a plain cross-site HTML form log the victim's browser into a session the attacker picked.

## Exploit scenario

An attacker who has an account on the same Unbind instance hosts a page that auto-submits <form method=POST enctype=application/x-www-form-urlencoded action=[https://unbind.victim.tld/.../auth/login](<https://unbind.victim.tld/.../auth/login>)> with email=attacker@x&password=... in a top-level window. Huma parses the form through urlEncodedFormat and Login issues the attacker's \__Host- session cookies (SameSite=Lax, which browsers accept on a top-level navigation response). The cookies replace the victim's session. The victim then works inside the attacker's account, for example entering variables or secrets, connecting repositories or deploying code that the attacker can later read.

## Preconditions

* Attacker has valid credentials on the same Unbind instance
* Victim visits an attacker-controlled page while able to reach the Unbind host

## Fix

Run originMatches on the unauthenticated state-changing /auth (and /setup, /invitations) routes, or reject any request body Content-Type other than application/json. Drop the global urlEncodedFormat unless an operation really needs it.

---

issues.title: [F83] Terminal websocket reads whole messages with no size limit (SetReadLimit never called)
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-770
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/terminal/exec.go:118` in `readPump`

## Impact

The shared API process can run out of memory and crash, a denial of service for all tenants. This is limited by the attacker's upload bandwidth: memory grows roughly in step with the bytes sent.

## What

The client sends the websocket frames, and readPump reads them with gorilla's ReadMessage, which does io.ReadAll on the full message. The upgrader and conn never call SetReadLimit, so readLimit stays 0, which means no limit. Gorilla's Upgrade also clears the HTTP server deadlines (server.go:265), so one huge or endlessly fragmented message is buffered in the API process without bound.

## Exploit scenario

A user with editor on a service that has a running pod opens /exec from a non-browser client and sets an allowed Origin header. They then send one binary websocket message, or a chain of continuation frames, totalling several gigabytes, across one or more connections. The API buffers each message in full before it writes anything to stdin, so its memory grows until the pod is OOM-killed.

## Preconditions

* Attacker is authenticated with editor on a service (Resolve permission check)
* The service has at least one pod
* Attacker can upload several GB to the API

## Fix

Call ws.SetReadLimit with a small bound (for example 64 KiB) right after Upgrade, and add a read deadline that the pong handler refreshes.

---

issues.title: [F84] Nil pointer dereference in an unrecovered webhook goroutine crashes the whole API process when the project lookup fails
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-476
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/services/project/update.go:85` in `UpdateProject`

## Impact

The API stops for every tenant of the shared platform, not only the attacker's team (availability). Confidentiality and integrity are not affected.

## What

Inside the fire-and-forget goroutine, `project, err := GetByID(..., project.ID)` declares a new `project` that shadows the outer one. When GetByID fails, for example with NotFound because a concurrent DeleteProject committed, that new `project` is nil. The error branch then reads `project.ID`, which panics. Nothing in the goroutine recovers, so the Go runtime ends the entire API process. CreateProject has the same defect at apps/api/internal/services/project/create.go:118.

## Exploit scenario

A user who is a team admin, and so may both update and delete projects, creates throwaway projects. For each one they send PUT update-project and DELETE project at the same moment. The update's UPDATE has to commit before the delete takes its row lock, and the goroutine's GetByID has to run after the delete commits. When both line up, GetByID returns NotFound and line 85 dereferences nil. The panic is outside any recover, so the unbind-api process exits, every in-flight request for every team fails, and the API is down until Kubernetes restarts the pod. The user can repeat this. A transient database error during GetByID has the same effect with no attacker involved. I inferred the race timing by reading the code and did not run it.

## Preconditions

* Authenticated user with editor on the project (update) and admin on the project (delete), or two cooperating users
* The update and delete requests must hit a narrow commit-ordering race, or GetByID must fail for another reason such as a database error

## Fix

In the error branch, log the outer ID that is already known, for example capture `projectID := project.ID` before `go func()` and log projectID, or stop shadowing the variable. Make the same change at project/create.go:118. Also consider adding a deferred recover to background webhook goroutines so a bug there cannot take down the API.

---

issues.title: [F85] Password change or admin reset does not revoke existing session refresh tokens
issues.description:
**Severity:** LOW (confidence medium), CWE-613
**Where:** `apps/api/internal/repositories/user/mutations.go:41` in `UpdatePassword`

## Impact

An attacker who already holds a session keeps account access after the victim or an admin rotates the password, which defeats the usual response to a compromise.

## What

UpdatePassword only rewrites password_hash. It does not revoke or delete the user's oauth2_tokens rows. Nothing in services/user/update.go does either: the only writes to Oauth2Token are CreateToken, RevokeAccessToken/RevokeRefreshToken (logout) and CleanTokenStore. The auth middleware keeps accepting any stored, unrevoked, unexpired refresh cookie and mints new access JWTs from it, so a stolen session outlives the credential rotation.

## Exploit scenario

An attacker gets a victim's refresh cookie, for example from a compromised browser or a shared machine. The victim notices and changes their password, or a system admin resets it. The attacker's refresh token is still valid, and for up to 14 days the middleware keeps issuing fresh access tokens that carry the victim's full permissions and Kubernetes group claims.

## Preconditions

* Attacker already holds a valid session refresh token for the victim
* Victim or admin changes the password to recover

## Fix

When the password changes (both self-service and admin reset), revoke every oauth2_tokens row for that user, for example with Update().Where(oauth2token.HasUserWith([user.ID](<http://user.ID>)(userID))).SetRevoked(true), in the same transaction as the hash update. Then issue a new session to the caller if needed.

---

issues.title: Sort metrics chart tooltip and legend by value
issues.description:
The tooltip on the metrics charts (memory, CPU, network, disk) lists series in the order the API returns them, not by value. With many services you can't tell at a glance what is using the most. In the screenshot, Banano Miner (1.8 GB) and Graham (1.3 GB) sit in the middle of the list, below Discord Invite (29 MB).

Expected:

* Tooltip rows sorted by the value at the hovered timestamp, largest first.
* Legend sorted the same way, by the latest value or the average over the window.

Notes:

* Chart lives in `apps/web/src/components/metrics/metrics-chart.tsx`. `ChartTooltip`/`ChartTooltipContent` render the rows with no sorting today.
* Recharts' `Tooltip` has an `itemSorter` prop, e.g. `itemSorter={(item) => -Number(item.value)}`. Not yet checked whether the shadcn `ChartTooltipContent` wrapper respects it.
* The legend order comes from the series config, so it would need sorting where the series list is built.
